The house resumed, from Friday, December 7, consideration of the motion of Hon. J. L. Ilsley (Minister of Finance) that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a measure to grant authority to accept on behalf of Canada and to carry out the obligations of Canada under the articles of agreement for an international monetary fund and an international bank for reconstruction and development prepared by the united nations monetary and financial conference held at Bretton Woods in July, 1944; to authorize the payment of the subscriptions required from Canada out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund to an amount not exceeding seven hundred million dollars; and to authorize the borrowing under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, of sums not exceeding seven hundred million dollars.
Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): Before I resume what I was in the process of saying about this matter last night, I should like to make one comment which I think should be considered by every member of this house. The Minister of Finance has stressed the objectives in the Bretton Woods plan. I quite appreciate that these objectives are worthy, and perhaps every member of the house will share that appreciation, but I want it definitely understood that we are concerned about the means by which the objectives are attained, and properly so. It is all very well to say that the best way to cure a headache is to cut off the patient's head, but we are opposed to cutting off the patient's head, and that is exactly the reason why we are trying to direct the attention of hon. members and of the people of the country to the means involved in bringing about the objectives that have been so admirably set out by the Minister of Finance.
When the debate was adjourned last night I was bringing before hon. members evidence of the industrial and economic unbalance between the United States and the rest of the world. I pointed out some statistical sum-47696-198J
maries that were published in the Fortnightly Review by Mr. R. P. Schwartz, an eminent authority on these matters. He concluded his statistical summary in connection with the matter of unbalances and the terrific economic industrial preponderance of the United States, in a world of smaller economies, by making this statement:
Upon the disappearance of this industrial and economic unbalance as between the United States and the rest of the world depends the economic recovery of the world.
If anyone has any doubts left in his mind concerning this economic unbalance and concerning what my hon. friend the member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) said the other night, when he referred to the United States as a giant among pygmies, as a Gulliver among the Lilliputians, when he said that this Gulliver, this tremendous giant in the world of economic and industrial affairs, would have to be very careful how he moved his foot lest some of the pygmies be crushed inadvertently, let me refer briefly to some further evidence of this great economic and industrial preponderance of the United States of America.
I have in my hand a treatise "America Conquers Britain", by Ludwell Denny, an eminent authority, and I suggest that the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), particularly, pay attention to what this author says. The hon. gentleman last night called me crazy when I said that the United Kingdom came cap in hand to the United States last September in her efforts to get assistance for post-war rehabilitation in that country. I suggest therefore that the hon. member read what Mr. Denny has to say and get the evidence which he presents in this book, "America Conquers Britain". If he does he will find out whether I was crazy. I suggest that to the hon. member for Melfort, who apparently is still living in the same fog that clouded his vision and understanding at the time that Britain needed our help in Canada during the early days of this war. I will quote briefly some of the things that Mr. Denny brings out.
I have heard members of the party to which the member for Melfort belongs decry, and rightly so, the grasp which the United States industrialists are securing in other countries. I have heard them mention, and rightly so, International Nickel, and many other things which United States industrial power is doing in our own country, Canada, and of the great control that they exercise over the Canadian economy. I want it definitely understood that the process of industrial conquest has been going on for many years in Britain and other countries until the
Bretton Woods Agreements

United States economic and industrial power has conquered Britain and many other parts of the empire with it.
Mr. Denny points out that in the United States during the boom period prior to 1929 the financiers were busy effecting great company mergers. He records that more than 1,000 public utility company mergers took place in the United States in 1926. In the period from 1927 to 1929 there were fifty bank mergers in New York alone, "creating an ever larger concentration of capital for domestic and foreign use," and he mentions that the National City bank had 98 branches in 26 foreign countries. What does that mean? From 1925 to 1928 United States loans to foreign countries averaged $1,100 million a year. Seventeen American corporations operating in foreign countries floated bond and stock issues in 1928 totalling $147 million. For what purpose? What would they be doing with this huge mobilization of the American public's money.
Mr. Denny supplies innumerable instances of what they are doing with it, of which the following are good examples. In 1929 General Motors of the United States bought the controlling interest in the Opel Motors of Germany. By March, 1929 American General Electric had bought sixty per cent of the stock of British General Electric, a controlling interest. Early in 1929 the leading electrical manufacturing concern in Britain, namely British Thompson Houston, Metropolitan Vicars, Edison, Swan, and Ferguson Pailin, were fused into the Associated Electrical Industries in which the principal shareholder was American General Electric.
I should like the member for Rosthern particularly to hear what I am saying because this should be impressed upon his mind after the demonstration he gave in this house last night.
Exhibition would be a better word, would it not?

I suppose exhibition would be appropriate. In 1928 Electric Bond and Share, subsidiary of American General Electric, more than doubled its investments-from $108 million to $285 million-in Britain through these and other concerns. General Electric is said to control fifty-two per cent of the United States total power production. The Bond and Share Subsidiary controls public utilities of eleven foreign countries and has large holdings in six other foreign countries.
Another point that Mr. Denny brings out forcibly is this. In Italy American General Electric is said to have large holdings in Italian Super Power, which is making that

country independent of British coal and has undoubtedly brought about a deterioration in the coal trade from Britain, which has brought her almost to her knees. American General Electric further interlocks with Radio Corporation of America, which in its turn is a huge trust with world-wide domination over wireless, the greatest means of mass communication in the entire world; and further, British Marconi Company is now tied up with Radio Corporation, of which I have just spoken. In 1929 American Power and Light Corporation brought up the entire common stock of greater London Counties Trust, a trust controlling seven of the chief power companies of Britain and supplying power on a monopoly basis to ninety-five cities in England and Scotland. It also controls Edmundson Electrical Corporation owning a number of electrical supply companies in Britain. A British government inquiry was made into this United States ownership of the motive power of British industry but it lamely reported that the ownership was unimportant. The late Lord Birkenhead was set up as a representative of the United States owners.
I could go on and enumerate hundreds of cases brought to light by Ludwell Denny showing and proving conclusively the almost complete conquest of Britain and the British commonwealth by United States industry.
Just at this point I should like to emphasize for the benefit of the hon. member for Ros-thern and the hon. member for Melfort that when we speak of Britain coming to the United States with cap in hand, when we speak of the tremendous preponderance of United States industry and productive capacity, we are not attacking Mr. Roosevelt, the late revered president of the United States. No one in this group has ever done so. I think the hon. member for Rosthern could have saved himself the wear and tear of his outburst last night in that connection. What we have tried to emphasize is that the preponderance of the United States in world industry and production has made it absolutely necessary that something be done to remove the unbalances, otherwise inadvertently they may cause the destruction of lesser countries of the world, I would remind the hon. member that when he speaks of Mr. Roosevelt as being a friend of Canada, I agree that he was. He was also a revered friend of Great Britain. But I should like to ask the hon. member for Rosthern, or anybody else for that matter, whether he thinks it would have been humanly possible for President Roosevelt, with all the multitudinous affairs of state that he had to look after, to go deeply into the implications of Bretton Woods and know all of them.

_______________Bretton Woods Agreements
I suggest that that would be foolish. President Roosevelt had to depend upon his advisers. I would like to know who those advisers were. I would like to know if Bernard Baruch was one. I know Morgenthau was one and there were several others. I suggest that those men were certainly looking after the welfare of the United States.
In that connection I am going to quote for the benefit of the hon. member for Rosthern what Mr. Morgenthau said at the Bretton M oods conference. I am quoting from the united nations monetary and financial conference Final Act, and related documents where Mr. Baruch is quoted on page 8. I suppose the hon. member for Rosthern was there and he probably heard him say this:
The American delegation, which I have had the honour of leading, has at all times been conscious of its primary obligation-the protection of American interests.
I suggest that the United States delegation have always had foremost in their minds the protection of United States interests. No one denies that they have been mighty hard bargainers in the past and they have not yet got over that mental complex by any means. That is the reason why this thing must be subjected to the most careful scrutiny to see to it that our interests have been carefully looked after. One question which I think ought to be answered in this house is whether the Canadian delegation amply and completely looked after Canadian interests.
I should like to know also whether the Bretton Woods agreements have any provision for reducing the preponderance of the United States in the industrial and productive fields to bearable proportions by ending existing economic inequalities between nations, which in the long run must of necessity produce not only adverse political reactions but adverse economic reactions throughout the world.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That is the basic idea underlying the whole agreement. When my hon. friend talks like that it makes me think that he has not studied the agreement at all.
The hon. member for Rosthern will have plenty of opportunity to present his evidence. I make the suggestion right now that he be ready to present that evidence in committee.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It is in the agreement itself.

I do not want him to do this from any hidden conception he may have in his own mind, but from the Final Act itself.
Does Bretton Woods provide and ensure that the United States will buy enough and can buy enough from its customers to give them regularly that supply of dollars which they require for their purchases from the United States? Upon a satifsactory answer to that question will depend whether I can support the measure. If the hon. member can show that it does, then fine.
Let me examine for just a moment the United States employment prospects, which reveal some very significant things. Competent authorities in the United States expect a very large unemployment problem by 1946 unless something adequate is done to prevent it. The Falk Foundation and other investigations carried on in the United States indicate that they expect unemployment to reach as high as 20,000,000 unless some very effective means are taken to provide relief. I suggest that if the United States is to avoid mass unemployment a far greater total of goods and services will have to be produced and consumed by Americans than ever before in peace time. Mr. Vinson, the new secretary of the treasury of the United States, recently described this-he shows by his statement that he understands the situation-as "the pleasant predicament of having to learn to live fifty per cent better than ever before." That must mean that he understands at least one great problem that has to be resolved before Bretton Woods can possibly be made to work.
The problem I say is one of matching expenditures to potential production. I suggest that it is not an insoluble problem, but it does require new vision and a new type of thinking. I have been much interested in some of the figures that have been given with respect to the prospects of full employment in the United States and also their great productive capacity. I should like to quote some figures which were recently published by the department of commerce with respect to the gross national product of the United States.
I find that in 1929, this gross national product measured in terms of market prices total $99-4 billion; by 1944 that had risen to $198-7 billion. It had almost doubled. In other words, the United States is producing to-day nearly twice as much goods and services as she did in any time of peace.
The explanation is not far to seek; it simply must be that there were unexpected and unexplained margins of employment where they could have put men to work and where in many instances they could have doubled the capacity of existing factories and industrial concerns. I am convinced that if the United States is to avoid unemployment, far larger
Bretton Woods Agreements

totals of goods and services will have to be produced and consumed in America than ever before in peace time.
What was their consumption in peace time? In 1929 the total consumption of gross national product in the three fields of ordinary consumption, government consumption and capital consumption was only $87-7 biEion. That was at the peak of the pre-war years. The consumption in 1944, which included war consumption, had risen to $171-2 billion. These recent surveys indicate that if the United States is to solve the unemployment problem that will face her as she goes into peace time she will have to keep up her gross national production to approximately $170 billion.
That poses a problem. It means that if the United States is going to keep her people busy, is going to give them what she pleases to call full employment-and I understand she is determined to do that-she will have to train her people to consume at least 50 per cent more goods and services within the country than they have ever consumed in any previous year. It means that the United States of America will have to find means of distributing equitably among its people purchasing power or consumer demand to enable them to consume those vast extra quantities of goods and services. Further, they will have to change a good many of their habits in some parts of the country to be able to do that, and this poses a problem that will have to be tackled before Bretton Woods can even start on the road to success.
In addition, even if the United States of America maintain a yearly gross national production of the S170 billion required to take care of the employment situation, and even if they train their people and make it possible through the distribution of effective consumer demand for their people to consume 50 per cent more than they have done in any year previously, there will still be left a great volume of goods, estimated variously at from four to seven billion dollars, that will have to go into the export market. If they do not make effective demand available to all the people of the United States and thus help to increase their internal consumption, it follows that a far larger total of the gross national production of the United States will be dumped into international trade channels, and when that happens in quantities greater than ever before, I suggest that it will bring about a very difficult problem in world affairs. I say that the solution of that problem cannot be found anywhere in Bretton Woods. I ask you,

Mr. Speaker, and through you the hon. members who are sponsoring this measure, what provision Bretton Woods is making to see to it that the people of the United States will receive internally, sufficient effective consumer demand to enable them to consume 50 per cent more per year than they ever consumed in their lives before. I suggest that there is nothing in Bretton Woods which indicates any attempt to make that possible.
In a lesser degree Canada is in the same position as is the United States. Canada, if it wishes to maintain fuU employment from now on, will have to increase the gross national production and the gross national consumption. The only way that can be done is to find some means of distributing effective consumer demand in this country to the people who need it so that Canadians can consume. Otherwise all this talk of adjusting trade on a multilateral basis is just so much quibble. If I can be assured that Bretton Woods provides some means whereby the United States can consume within that country most of the goods she produces, or if it provides that the great exportable surplus that must be available if they put their men to work, may be given away or put into the hands of the peoples of the more unforunate countries of the world without piling up against them unpayable burdens of debt, I will support it.
Much has been said about gold and the gold standard. I am not certain in my own mind what kind of gold standard this might introduce. But it does seem queer that concurrently with the drive to get Bretton Woods adopted by the house and by the government, there has been a protracted programme of propaganda on the part of K. V. Gamble Company in Toronto to show that a gold standard is necessary. That may be just accident; I do not know. Here are some of the headlines: "Gold is the Balance Wheel of International Trade"-"That Off The Gold Standard Urge"-"A Herculean Task Requires Herculean Methods"-"The Old Lady Goes to Work," and so on. Of course, it may be just accident that these pamphlets appear just at this time; I do not know.
There are five points in connection with the gold standard which I should like hon. members to consider. The five points follow: Whether Bretton Woods means the introduction of a gold standard similar to the one of 1925 or 1914 I do not know, but the fact remains that:

Bretton Woods Agreements
i(l) Under the old gold standard the value of sterling was legally fixed in terms of a given weight of gold. This will be precisely the same under the new gold standard.
(2)	Under the old gold standard our monetary authorities were under the obligation to buy and sell gold freely at a fixed buying and selling price.
This will be the same under the new gold standard, with the difference that gold will not be available for internal hoarding.
(3)	Under the old gold standard sterling was allowed to fluctuate within a range of about one per cent. Under the new gold standard its range of fluctuations has been rigidly fixed at one per cent.
(4)	Under the old gold standard there was no .limit for the fluctuation of the price of sterling for future delivery. In this respect the new gold standard is much more rigid, for under it a limit will be set also to the fluctuations of "forward" sterling.
(5)	Under the old gold standard it was possible for this country to suspend the system or to devalue sterling to any extent by simple government decision, subject .to confirmation by parliament, without having to ask for the permission of any outside body, indeed, without having to consult anybody about it.
Under the new gold standard, on the other hand, it will be necessary to obtain the permission of an international board, on which our trade rivals will control the majority vote for any devaluation in excess of 10 per cent.
These are not my opinions; they are the opinions of an expert. The five points I have just quoted are the opinion of Professor Paul Einzig.
May I assure the minister in conclusion that I am prepared to support what he has asked. No further speakers from this group will take part in the debate at this stage, but I should like the assurance on a matter of such import-* ance as this not only that it will be given ample consideration by the banking and com-eeree committee but that we shall be given the opportunity for full debate also in this house in committee of the whole when the measure comes back from the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

With your permission, Mr. Speaker, and the permission of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Low) I should like to ask him a question, not in any spirit of opposition, because I agree with a great deal of the data which he has placed before the house and which I think is not open to question. But I think there is a point of difference between my hon. friend and myself in the matter of philosophy. I think he has come a long way tc.ward my views, and I want to make sure whether I am right. The hon. gentleman made much in his argument of the ownership of industrial control by the United States of America, and made special reference to the ownership by the Americans of a large proportion of the electric power available in Great Britain. My understanding of his philosophy is that he takes the position that in Canada it does not matter who owns anything so long as those who do own it produce, that so long as we get the goods it does not matter who owns anything. If it does not matter who owns anything in Canada, by what reasoning, I would ask, does he arrive at the conclusion that it makes any difference who owns anything in the other nations of the world?

It ought to be obvious to the hon. member that in the international sphere the ownership can create these unfavourable trade balances which Bretton Woods is supposed to be ready to cure. But internally, that is nationally, I would say that the government of this country ought to be in a position to provide the capital to buy out international cartels and combines, and afterwards sell them into the hands of private ownership, to see that they are properly run.
That is socialism.
No.
Social ownership.
You did not get the last part of the sentence: "in the hands of private ownership", he said.

When I spoke on December 6, the Finance Minister asked me the following question at the conclusion of my remarks:
What is the authority for the hon. member's statement that the United States forced a promise from Mr. Winston Churchill that he would lead the United Kingdom back to a gold standard satisfactory to the United States?
I replied:
I explained at the outset what my authority was. I was giving it for what it is worth. The pamphlet was signed by Mr. Eric Troward, president of the liberator council, and it is headed:
This memorandum has been specially prepared for the benefit of new members of parliament, many of whom have not had the opportunity of studying the trend of international financial development during the past two years.
In regard to the liberator council, I would just like to point out that the chief adviser is Sir Charles Morgan-Webb, late chief secretary of the Burma government, who is a world authority on gold and the sterling group. So it is not a pamphlet that can be dismissed lightly. I do not think a man like Sir Charles Morgan-Webb would have anything to do with an organization distributing .a pamphlet making that charge unless there was some proof of it.
Mr. Usley:	My hon. friend is basing its
authenticity upon the alleged standing of the adviser to this liberator council. As to who the gentleman is who made the statement, I do not know. I just want to say that I do not believe the statement.
Mr. Quelch:	The minister will agree that the
fact that Britain has agreed to Bretton Woods is pretty good backing for that statement.
Mr. Ilsley:	No, I do not believe that the
dominions of the British empire are joining in this treachery to themselves. I think that is ridiculous.
I wrant to deal for a few minutes with the two points raised by the minister in this question. I should like to take the last statement first, in which the minister said he did not believe the dominions of the British empire were joining in this treachery to themselves, that it was ridiculous. Just to make sure there is no misunderstanding of what I might mean by the term "treachery" I should like to give the definition from Webster's dictionary, which says it is a violation of faith and confidence, or perfidious action, and of course I was referring to it in that sense. I believe I can justify my stand in that regard. I am not suggesting for one moment that the people of the dominions are betraying themselves, but what I do suggest is that the governments, under the advice of certain experts, are taking action that will be highly detrimental to the

Bretton Woods Agreements
countries concerned, and to that extent will unquestionably be a breach of the confidence they have from the people. As to who advises the experts of course I am not in a position to say. I think the committee would be very glad if the minister would explain exactly how this whole thing originated. Who was responsible for this? Did it come from the government in the first place, or did it come as a recommendation from some other body? I understand that the government participated in certain agreements at London and Washington to set up some form of monetary stabilization, and some time ago I asked what were the terms of reference upon which our experts worked. Did they go there with a completely free hand to agree to an international standard based upon gold, or was it recommended that they advocate a multilateral system of trade using the national currencies of the countries based upon index price levels rather than in terms of gold? I believe later on the minister should explain that point; I have asked the question before, but up to the present have not been able to obtain an answer.
I think the minister will agree that in the past there has been every reason why, not only in this country but in every country in the world, we should have a good deal of misgiving in regard to the actions or recommendations of so-called experts. I am going to give the minister two or three notable examples of what I am referring to. First of all I should like to mention the statement in Mr. Churchill's speech in 1932, when he said:
When I was moved by many .arguments and forces in 1925 to return to the gold standard I was assured by the highest experts, and our experts are men of great ability and of indisputable integrity and sincerity-
Then some one said, "And they are always wrong." Mr. Churchill went on:
The hon. member is not always right-that we were anchoring ourselves to reality and stability; and I accepted their advice.
What did he find?
I take for myself and my colleagues of other days whatever degree of blame and burden there may be for having accepted their advice.
He takes responsibility for having accepted the advice and goes on to say:
But what has happened? We have had no reality, no stability. The price of gold has risen since then by more than seventy per cent. That is as if a twelve-inch foot rule had suddenly been stretched to nineteen or twenty inches; as if the pound avoirdupois had suddenly become twenty-three or twenty-four ounces instead of-how much is it?-sixteen.
I need not put more of that statement on record. I quote it to show that Mr. Churchill
took the advice of men supposed to be real experts, and the advice proved to be faulty. Then I recall the actions of one man of world renown, the former governor of the Bank of England, Montagu Norman. I have not his statement here, but I have quoted it in the house before and I will just repeat it from memory. I took it from the British Hansard in 1939. He stated that he had made loans to Germany and said, "We may never get those loans back, but it would be better to lose that money than to see the fall of nazism." Imagine the head of the Bank of England, one of the chief advisers on monetary affairs, saying they had made loans of money to Germany and might never get the money back but it would be better to lose it than to see the fall of nazism! Was that sound advice? Would not the minister consider that was unquestionably treachery to the nation? I do not say that at the time Montagu Norman made that statement he intended to commit an act of treachery or to betray England. He may have held that there were other dangers and therefore it was better to build up Germany as a bulwark, but in view of what happened later I think everyone will agree that his action rebounded against Britain, because within a short time we had to defend ourselves against Germany.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Could we not shorten this discussion by my admission that experts are sometimes wrong, and by my hon. friend's admission that they are sometimes right?

I do not need the second part of that statement, but I am very glad to hear the minister make that admission,, and I hope he will impress that fact upon the hon. member for Rosthern, who on two occasions in this house has told us what a marvellous man Keynes is, and that as far as he is concerned if Keynes has said this is not the gold standard he is prepared to accept it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I think Keynes is one of the outstanding economists in the world today, and is so regarded by other economists.
Yes, and so were these other experts whose advice Churchill took in 1925.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: He did not take that advice from Keynes.

Norman was supposed to be an outstanding expert. In reference to Keynes I believe the hon. member was in the house when the then hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard quoted a statement by Keynes; and we all remember the reply given at that time by Mr. Dunning. I do not have it here, but you will remember he said in
Bretton Woods Agreements

effect: Why should we be asked to accept the word of Maynard Keynes? He has gone back on all his former convictions.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: As the hon. member knows, I did not happen to agree with Mr. Dunning in that attitude.
Who has the floor?

Let him talk; probably I would not have thought of that if the hon. member had not been talking. However, the Minister of Finance has given in rather easily on this point, and I am glad to have his admission in regard to the experts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should like to have yours.

We will give you ours before we are through; we have given our views before, but in view of the fact that undoubtedly this bill will eventually reach the banking committee I think perhaps it would be better for us to wait until it is there before we do give our views. In the meantime we have many questions to ask, for the simple reason that we should like to have a statement from the minister before we are asked to give our views on the matter. After all, this is his responsibility. He has accepted the advice of these people, and he must be prepared to back up the action he has taken. Therefore we want to see whether his replies correspond with those of the experts.
Perhaps I should say a further word in regard to the statement made just now by the minister that the experts are not always right. Let me remind him of what happened in this country. The minister, said we could give our advice, too. Well, we did give our advice in 1936 and 1939, and events proved that our advice was right and that the advice given by the experts was totally wrong. Let us remember what happened back in 1932, when Germany and Japan started to rearm. Russia was arming also, because she knew that eventually she would have to defend herself against Germany and Japan, but what did the British empire do? It took the advice of experts and imposed a deflationary policy. It cut down employment, increased unemployment, put people on relief, and as a result when war came thousands of men had to be discharged because of malnutrition. Was that just an accident? When our potential enemies were all rearming, was it simply an accident that we imposed a deflationary policy and deliberately sabotaged the resources of the empire? I cannot believe it was entirely accidental. I think there was something definitely sinister behind that procedure.
Sinister is right.
I am not suggesting that the experts in the department were responsible, but I believe that there are experts from whom they obtained further advice.
Or instructions.

I recall that some time ago I asked that certain correspondence between the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England be tabled and I was told that it would not be in the interests of the dominion to table it. It was probably not in the interests of the banks to table that correspondence, but it might have been in the interests of Canada to have it brought down. I recall when talking about reconstruction once I pointed out that we were definitely paving the way for the restoration of gold and the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) rose in his place and said no. Is he prepared to say that to-day?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
Does he say that we are not going to establish currency at the par value of gold?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Which gold standard is my hon. friend referring to-gold exchange or gold reserve?

I am not referring to 1914 or 1925. I am referring to the fact that article IV, section 1, states that the par value of the currency of each member shall be expressed in terms of gold as the common denominator, or in terms of the United States dollar, and so on. As one hon. member said the other night, that is not the standard that he wishes to go back to; the gold standard for him is the turkey standard that he established in depression years. The member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) eulogized at some length the work of the experts at Bretton Woods. I do not doubt that there were very capable men there. The hon. gentleman said that he had seen them in action. Apparently the jargon of the experts rather hypnotized him, and after listening to that jargon he became very greatly impressed. I can quite understand that when some experts get going the effect is hypnotic. I was not on the banking committee last year because I was serving on the committee on reconstruction, but I remember going one day to one of the meetings of the banking committee and there I saw in action a gentleman by the name of Tompkins, I believe. I do not know his exact name. Well, he was a wow. Acrobats on the stage had nothing on him. I had seen acrobats on the stage tie themselves into knots, but the3r were always able to get out of their

Bretton Woods Agreements
difficulties. They could untie themselves. This gentleman, however, kept tying himself into a tighter and tighter knot and he was never able to get out of it. I am satisfied that if he had been asked' to give a definition of a straight line, instead of defining it as the shortest distance between two points, he would have defined every other sort of line he could think of and in the end would have failed to define a straight line. Everyone who was on that committee will, I believe, agree with that statement. I think the Minister of Finance will agree that the statements made by that expert were about as confusing as they could possibly be. Every time he made a statement it took an hour or two for the members of the committee to understand what he was driving at. That is all I have to say about *experts.
Now I should like to say a few words about the Liberator Council. I am not blaming the minister for being sceptical. Perhaps he has never heard of this council but in view of the fact that it is a body of men who have been doing excellent work in England, working in close cooperation with the Economic Reform Club, I suggest that no one should dismiss their views lightly. I have already mentioned Sir Charles Morgan-Webb. Perhaps I might give the names of the five men comprising the council: Sir Geoffrey Bracken, Mr. William Brown, Mr. G. H. Stock, Sir. Charles Morgan-Webb and Mr. Eric Troward. They have put up a fight against Bretton Woods from the start. They organized meetings all across England and some time ago organized a large meeting known as the Bayswater conference at which Mr. Craven Ellis, M.P. and Mr. Stokes, M.P., participated in the debate. At that meeting they discussed four alternatives: The Twentieth Century economic plan of the London Chamber of Commerce; the Volens System, the McCarron Plan and the Liberator system. I have read all these, but the only one I have tried to understand is the London Chamber of Commerce plan, because I find it easier to follow. At the meeting in the evening session there were *over 350 persons present, with 44 diplomatic and consular representatives. There were 28 nations represented altogether, so that the minister will agree that it was no fly-by-night concern but a reputable organization doing a great deal of very valuable work.
And now I should like to say a few words on the gold standard. Article IV, section 1, provides that the par value of the currency of each member shall be expressed in terms of gold as a common denominator, or in terms of the United States dollar of the weight and fineness in effect on July 1, 1944. Section 3 *states that the maximum and minimum rates
for exchange transactions between the currencies of members taking place within their territories shall not differ from parity, in the case of spot exchange transactions by more than one per cent, and in the case of other exchange transactions by a margin which exceeds for spot exchange transactions by more than the fund considers reasonable. It is also provided that there shall be a change in par value of members' currency up to ten per cent without any need of consulting the fund, but if a nation goes beyond that, the fund must be consulted. I was interested to know what the orthodox definition of gold standard would be, and I looked up the Encyclopedia Britannica and I found that a nation's money, paper bills and silver coins, when that nation is on the gold standard, are redeemable at a fixed weight of fine gold for each monetary unit. One might say that is not true in all essentials of the Bretton Woods agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not in any essential. Why does my hon. friend crawl out and say not in all essentials?

Let me finish my sentence. The main point is that the results of the operation of the system will have very much the same effect as the gold standard, for this reason. Under the automatic clause of the gold standard in the old days if a nation had an unfavourable balance of trade, gold went out of the country, with the result that there was a credit restriction and the price level fell, and then as a result of the fall in price level, which was supposed to encourage other nations to buy their goods, the price level in other countries went up and after a while nations stopped buying their goods, with the result that they had an unbalance of trade. It was supposed to act as an automatic regulator. But what happened if a nation was not willing to reduce its price level? It might have been all right in olden days to tell a nation that if it did not have gold it would have to reduce its price level no matter how great its powers of production might be. That was all right then, but people are not quite so foolish as to believe that argument any more. Mr. T. E. Gregory, in his book "The Gold Standard and its Future," points out what happens, and I quote from page 32:
Thirdly, the world economic structure has become rigid to an unprecedented degree. Owing to the much greater pressure which organized business and labour interests can bring to bear on government, there has been a general advocacy of "stability" which has an practice meant that particular groups could stabilize their own position without any, or enough, attention having been paid to the result of such stabilizing .action on other parts of the economic field or to the long period results of such action. Raw material producers have been allowed, with
Bretton Woods Agreements

the aid of governmental or quasi-governmental assistance, to "stabilize" the prices of particular raw materials, without regard to the fact that consumption might thereby be discouraged and production encouraged. In industry and distribution there has been a growth of large-scale organizations which have not always been willing to adjust prices to the trend of the market, thus adding in the end to the losses which had to be suffered on stocks when liquidation finally became necessary. In the sphere of labour there has been in certain countries a development of unemployment insurance schemes or similar relief measures which have prevented wage rates from falling, whilst in others public opinion, reinforced by government propaganda, has had very much the same effect. In a word, there have been tendencies at work in many countries preventing a rapid adjustment of the level of money incomes to changes in the general economic situation.
When people refuse to allow prices to fall then the gold standard is no longer able to operate automatically. If a nation continues to have an unfavourable balance of trade, the only alternative is to borrow money or to obtain gold. It can use the gold it has on hand, but if it does not have gold it will have to go further into debt. What is the effect under this agreement? If a nation has an unfavourable balance of trade it can borrow and go into debt. It can draw on its quota but when that is exceeded by 200 per cent it has reached the limit and it cannot borrow any further. It would not have any gold and the result is that in all probability it would cease to use the fund.
Neither under the gold standard nor under the Bretton Woods agreement does the creditor nation accept any responsibility for helping to balance the trade between nations. After all, the only way in which a debtor nation can pay is with its own goods. All a debtor nation should have to do is to say to a creditor nation, "We owe you $100 million; we have placed to your credit in the bank $100 million; with that you can buy any goods we have." That is all that nation should be required to do. Unfortunately that has not been the case and the result is that nations have been forced into a state of unpayable debt.
I am quite aware that under the Bretton Woods agreements when a nation's currency becomes scarce, provision is made for the fund to buy that scarce currency with gold, but that does not ease the situation so far as the individual nations are concerned. The only way they will be able to get goods is by going into debt if they have no gold with which to buy currency. I will quote article VII which deals with this question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
When the hon. member suggests that that is the only resort set up under this agreement, he is saying less than

what is correct. The fundamental basis of this organization is that if a currency becomes scarce then 'the country whose currency has become scarce will be advised by the officials of the fund that they must take steps to enable other countries to sell their goods in the country of the scarce currency, and they would advise that country that they must be prepared to correct that fundamental unbalance of trade. The whole basis of this agreement is designed to promote understanding between countries in order to permit balanced trade and the keeping up of high standards of living in all countries.
If the hon. member can show me any clause in the act that compels the creditor nation to do that, I shall be glad to see it. All it provides for is the rationing of scarce currency.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Does the hon. member suggest that this international body should interfere with the sovereignty of this country and compel us to do something rather than just urge us to do it?
I am suggesting that as long as it has the power to take action against a debtor nation, it should have the same power to take action against a creditor nation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has no power to take any action against a debtor nation. No debtor nation has to buy currencies from this fund.
What is the purpose of the fund? To expand trade?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is expected that they will, of course.

To expand trade on a multilateral basis. If a creditor nation refuses to buy goods in exchange for its exports, how is a debtor nation going to pay? You must make it possible for the weaker nations to be able to pay for their imports and exports, and yet this does not provide for that. All it does is to impose penalties on the debtor nations. Doctor Clark admitted in the committee that there is nothing in here to compel a creditor nation to buy goods.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What committee is that?
The reconstruction committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is this another conversation the hon. member had with the deputy minister?
The minister will find it on the record.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I want to protest against the hon. gentleman talking about conversations

Bretton Woods Agreements
that he had with the deputy minister in the corridors. I am not going to take the time to go back to the deputy minister to find out what was his recollection of the conversation. We had the hon. member for Wetaskiwin telling us last night that he could not break a confidence, that he could not tell us who his anonymous informant was about the ownership of gold in the United States. I want to say right now that I stand by what I said two or three years ago. I have given my authority as against the anonymous authority which the hon. gentleman has quoted. Yet the hon. member for Acadia stands up here and retails corridor conversations with one of my officials.

Wait a minute. The reference I made to the corridor conversation was not in any shape or form detrimental to Doctor Clark, and I am satisfied he would be quite prepared to have me repeat the statement.. In committee he was asked a question by Senator McGeer and he said he would study the London chamber of commerce proposals and give a report on them. Apparently lack of time made it impossible for him to do this and I merely asked him what his recollection was. He certainly did not tell me that he was speaking in confidence. He said he thought the proposals were quite good but the main difficulty was that several nations would not agree to them. I am quite sure that he would not object to my having repeated that statement. I asked what he thought of Russia, and he went on to say that he thought the country that would most strongly object to the proposals was the United States of America.
So far as the statement I am giving now is concerned, any member who was present in the reconstruction committee will recall the conversation with Doctor Clark. He said that he did not think we should impose, just as the hon. member for Rosthern is saying, conditions upon creditor nations.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: May I ask a question?

Let me finish with the
other question the hon. member asked. Section 8 of article V deals with the member nation which is unable to meet its obligations. Perhaps I had better read the whole section, otherwise I shall be charged with taking something out of its text. This section reads:
(c) The fund shall levy charges uniform for all members which shall be payable by any member on the average daily balances of its currency held by the fund in excess of its quota. These charges shall be .at the following rates:
(i)	On amounts not more than twenty-five per cent in excess of the quota: no charge for the first three months; one-half per cent per
annum for the next nine months; and thereafter an increase in the charge of one-half per cent for each subsequent year.
(ii)	On amounts more than twenty-five per cent and not more than fifty per cent in excess of the quota: an additional one-half per cent for the first year; and an additional one-half per cent for each subsequent year.
(iii)	On each .additional bracket of twenty-five per cent in excess of the quota: an additional one-half per cent for the first year; and an additional one-half per cent for each subsequent year.
(d) Whenever the fund's holdings of a member's currency are such that the charge applicable to any bracket foT any period has reached the rate of four per cent per annum, the fund and the member shall consider means by which the fund's holdings of the currency can be reduced. Thereafter, the charges shall rise in accordance with the provisions of (c) above until they reach five per cent and failing agreement, the fund may then impose such charges as it deems appropriate.
I suggest that that is a very severe penalty to impose on any debtor nation, to say that as you are not able to meet your obligations, the fund when your debt rises to a certain point can charge you any rate of interest it likes. If the members want me to do it I will read the whole of section 4.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
The whole purpose of that
section is to discourage a member from trying to finance a very heavy excess of imports over exports out of the fund. In other words the fund is to finance current transactions, not to finance capital expenditures. Its whole purpose is to discourage that very thing and to have it done by balancing trade.
How can you balance trade if one nation insists on exporting more than it imports? There is a mutual obligation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: The very fact of the nations coming together and making this agreement presupposes their willingness to balance their exports and imports. That was the basic supposition on which they met.
Where is all the gold?
May I ask a question?
These members don't know shucks about this thing. Let them live and learn.

Let me proceed. I quoted from a statement made by Doctor Clark the other day showing what Canada aims to be. The member for Rosthern says that the whole idea behind Bretton Woods is the balancing of trade. Here is what Doctor Clark said in a speech that he made in New York:
We feel also that adequate arrangements .are essential to make possible a substantial volume of long-term international investment, and we
Bretton Woods Agreements

trust that the technical and political difficulties involved in consummating these may soon be surmounted.
I agree that there is justification for investment on moral grounds, to help certain backward countries, but we knew how in days past there have been trade wars because nations tried to force their goods on other nations and then raised high tariffs to prevent those debtor nations from paying them with goods. The white paper on reconstruction which was issued last year by the Minister of Reconstruction stated that Canada in all probability would be a creditor nation. So apparently it is not expected that we are going to balance our trade but rather that we will maintain a favourable balance of trade and make loans through the international bank.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: These are loans to be made for reconstruction and development to enable a country to increase its productive power and raise its own standard of living so that it will be able to pay for its imports from other countries. They are productive loans.
Provided that it could sell the goods.

That is a lovely story, but I read how England had maintained her prosperity and that Mr. Reginald McKenna said that the reason England was prosperous for two centuries before 1914 was that she had been able to maintain a favourable balance of trade. The money paid for her goods exported abroad enabled her to maintain an effective demand for the goods retained internally. Owing to the fact that without exports there was no effective demand internally, Britain, in order to maintain full employment, found it necessary to export her surplus production abroad. Now the hon. member for Rosthern says that all we have to do is to make it possible for other nations to produce goods, and then there will be more prosperity. How are we going to export more abroad if we put other nations on a self-sustaining basis?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Each nation will make the goods it can best produce. That is the basis of international trade.

Have we in the past been able to maintain an effective demand against our production? Has the United States? The United States to-day is looking for large export markets. Why did Doctor Clark consider that it was necessary to make adequate arrangements for long-term foreign investments? Because he knows that we in this country are not able to maintain an effective demand against our total production, and so long as

that condition obtains the only way in which we can maintain full employment is to export abroad a certain amount of our production in excess of our imports.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Does not the hon. member admit that if we helped to set up China and develop her production and a high standard of living there, she could absorb all our export food products without any difficulty?

On the condition that we accept in return payment from China in manufactured goods; and if we have a deficiency in purchasing power in Canada to buy our total home production how are we going to be able to buy those imports from China? It has not been done in the past. We have argued, and this is the whole basis of our philosophy, that you have to maintain production at full capacity and then maintain an effective demand against that production, or against the production of other countries for which your own can be exchanged. But that has not been done in the past.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: The Bretton Woods proposals do not in any way interfere with the promotion of your doctrine within the country.
Nor with any other doctrine that will distribute goods.

If the hon. member is really sincere in his argument-and I think he is, although I doubt the sincerity of some people behind Bretton Woods-if the idea behind it all is to bring about a balance of trade, then the creditor nations as a sign of their sincerity should be willing to have included a section such as that which is included in the London chamber of commerce proposals, and the same suggestion was made in the Keynes plan. He mentioned that there should be an obligation on the part of creditor nations to accept payment in goods. There is nothing in these proposals at all to compel a creditor nation to accept payment in goods. But there is provision in here to force a debtor nation to pay any rate of interest that the fund sees fit to charge, after the debtor nation has gone into debt by a certain amount and for a certain period of time.
May I ask a question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member who has the floor will permit a question it may be asked.

I have had a lot of questions asked me and now I should like first of all to ask the Minister of Finance a question. I think the Minister of Finance will agree

Bretton Woods Agreements
with the soundness of the argument that there is a dual responsibility in regard to international trade, that it should be a two-way street. It should not merely be the purpose of international trade to dump our unemployment problem on the doorstep of some other nation. If we export goods we should be prepared to accept payment in imports; for that is the only way in which other nations can pay. Is the minister prepared then to say that there is an obligation to raise the purchasing power of the people of this country up to the point where they can buy the total production of Canada and the imports of other nations exchanged for our exports? If the minister will announce that as a policy for the future, and if the government will say to the industrial concerns throughout Canada that from now on they can expand their production to the full capacity, and will guarantee a market for their output, we shall have the greatest expansion the country has ever seen. And you would never need to worry about unemployment in the future, because you would put money into circulation so that the people could buy the goods which industry could produce

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The government has repeatedly announced that it is its policy to encourage enterprise and develop full employment.

But how is it going to do it?
Mr. Q'UELCH: That does not answer the question at all. "Encourage"!
Will it give a dividend?

I am not now asking a question as to the dividend. All I am asking for is a clear-cut statement from the government that they recognize a joint responsibility, as between the creditor and the debtor nations, to balance trade; that they recognize that the only way in which that can be achieved is by a nation setting its own house in order so that it will be willing and ready to take an equal quantity of imports for its exports, and so that the people will be able to buy the total production of the country. Is the minister prepared to agree to that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is different from the last question.
No, it is the same thing. I put the questions slightly differently, but they are the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And it is not clear, either.
I will state it again.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is my hon. friend asking that we recognize an obligation with respect to any particular country with which we are dealing, to take the same volume of imports that that country takes of exports from us? If so, we do not recognize that obligation at all. That is bilateralism, so-called.

I am not advocating bilateral trade. The minister must be familiar with the London chamber of commerce proposals. No doubt he has read them. I know that his department has studied them, because the deputy minister told me so. The London chamber of commerce proposals are a multilateral system. Money is not based on gold. It is tied to the price index level. Every country agrees to maintain its price level stable. Every country agrees to balance its trade and to maintain a stable rate of exchange between its currency and the currency of another nation. In view of the fact that a country agrees to maintain its price level stable, then when it buys any goods from another country, thereby obtaining that country's currency it knows that its money will buy a certain quantity of goods to-day and the same quantity a year hence. There is a definite undertaking to balance trade, and therefore any nation which over a period of seven years refuses to accept payment in goods has its credit wiped out. Then there is an international exchange established, and representatives of foreign exchange controls in every nation will sit on that exchange, exchanging their blocked credits for the blocked credits of other nations, and the nations will always know in which countries they have credits, so that they will endeavour to accept more imports from that nation. But it will be on a multilateral basis, because the representatives of the foreign exchange controls will be sitting on this exchange, trading the blocked credits. They will not have the power to change the value of a nation's currency. The exchange rate will be fixed in terms of the nation's price level, and gold will not enter into the question at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What is the question now? Is it changed?

The question is whether or not this government is prepared to guarantee to the industry of Canada that it will maintain the purchasing power of the people on a level which will make it possible for them to buy the total production of the country, and the production of other countries for which our own production may be exchanged.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is a guarantee that the government will issue money to the people
Bretton Woods Agreements

of Canada if they require it to buy all the goods they need from this country or other countries; is that it?
Not necessarily. Repeat that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I don't know whether I can repeat it. My hon. friend can never repeat his questions in the same language.
I am putting it in another way-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am wondering what sort of guarantee my hon. friend is asking me to make on behalf of the government. It sounded to me very much like this, that we would issue money
He did not mention "money".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does it mean that? I think that is what it means, and I think if I said "yes", that is what he would say we were committed to.

That all depends. The government Would estimate the total production of the country. They would estimate the approximate amount of labour required to produce the goods the people needed. They would know how much labour was available for various national projects. They would place a fair price on agricultural products. They -would guarantee a minimum standard of living to all people; we will say, in the initial stages, SI,200 a year. They would, as the leader of this group stated, grant old age pensions at sixty years at $50 a month. They would make grants available to all people up to the age of twenty-one, or any age necessary to complete their training so long as these young people showed that they had the ability to continue their studies. Then they could watch the effect; and if they found that demand still lagged behind supply, say that over a period of six months they found that production was still going ahead of consumption, they could establish a discount, which would be nothing more than a sales tax in reverse, in order to bring about a balance. In other words, using figures, if the amount of goods available during a period was equal to $10 million and the demand against those goods equal to only $9 million, showing a lag of ten per cent, for the next period a ten per cent discount would be established to bring demand up to supply, that is to establish equation. That would cover your exports and imports. So far as the issuing of money is concerned, the issuance of money would be only to the extent to which taxa-
tion failed to meet government expenditures; in that event national money would be used. If taxation was sufficient it would not be done. But the government would not be trying to limit its expenditures to the amount of money it, could tax from the people's pockets.
On that basis the government talks a lot about "full employment", a lot about "a new social order". They talk about "encouraging" this or that. Is it not time we have a government which would guarantee that it could take certain definite steps in order to promote the full development of the resources of the country? I think the minister will agree that the only way you can maintain full development of the country's resources is to guarantee a full-time market. The minister will agree that industry cannot continue to produce unless it can sell the goods it produces. Is the minister prepared to say that the government will in the future underwrite an effective demand in Canada? If a government will not do it, nobody else will.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the purport of the hon. gentleman's question is to commit the government to the detailed programme he outlined there, I say no. It is a long list of discounts and dividends and bonuses-
I never mentioned dividends.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -and so on. We cannot commit ourselves to that.
Then you are heading for chaos.

I am not asking the minister to commit himself to all this. The minister asked me what I suggest. I am giving him a suggestion. I am not tying him to details; the government can use any technique it likes. All we are interested in is results. The people are interested in seeing that their standard of living is maintained at the highest level that the production of the country can provide. What has happened in the past is that when effective demand fell, prices were not reduced to a level where people could buy the production, but second>-ary industries reduced their production in consequence of the inadequate buying power. Then what happened? Well, we know what happened from 1935 to 1939. All I am asking the minister is whether the government will, by any technique they choose, underwrite an effective demand against the production of the country. We are not indulging merely in negative criticism. At any time that we criticize the government we are prepared to put forward some alternative suggestion.

Would the minister give us some idea of the incidence of hog cholera during the last year?

There were no serious
outbreaks of hog cholera during last year. There was an outbreak in Manitoba. A number of hogs were slaughtered in Ontario during 1944-45 because of hog cholera. The figures are as follows: 1944-45. 494; 1943-44, 67; 1942-43, 3,415; 1941-42, 6,437. The figure was very much higher in 1940-41, 33,793. It will be noted that the tendency has been downwards.
Mr. HA.RRIS (Danforth):	In what part
of Ontario was the disease prevalent?

I am not certain as
to the exact place, but I think the greater
part of it was in the southwestern section of Ontario. The figures for Manitoba are as follows: In 1942-43, 83; 1943-44, 330; in 1944-45, 1,753. It will be noted that there is an increase there rather than a decrease.

Cattle prices have increased
materially during the past few years. Has the department given any consideration to changing the amounts that are paid to individuals whose cattle are slaughtered under the tuberculosis regulations? The amounts paid at the present time are comparatively small, something like $40 for a grade animal and around $100 for a pure bred animal. Has the department given any consideration to the matter, or does it intend to do anything about it?

No, we have not done
anything about it. The amount has remained about the same over a period of about twenty years. Experience has shown that while the maximum amounts which may be paid have remained constant, the amount which the farmer receives for anything that he can market goes up with the increase in the price of the animal. When prices are high he is able to sell part of the animal which has been condemned at a much higher price than when prices are low. We have had arguments when the prices were low and high to the effect that the amounts should be changed, but we have maintained the level over about a twenty-year period, and at the moment we are not considering changing it.

I was hopeful
that the department might take under advisement next session the matter of changing this compensation in view of the fact that prices are relatively high at the present time as compared with the twenty-year period of which the minister speaks. What is particularly running throuh my mind at the moment is the reference which was made by the hon. member for Lanark with regard to Bang's disease and tuberculosis contracted by humans from cattle. Compensation paid for these diseased cattle ought to be given some consideration so that we may clean up the unhealthy spots from which the disease emanates. If that were done it would benefit the general economy of Canada.

I think the whole question with regard to whether we are going to pay for Bang's disease as well as tuberculosis should be considered along with the other question when it comes up. Probably this is a matter to which we might give some consideration in the future. The hon. member
Supply-Agriculture

for Frontenac-Addington intimated to me that he was going to ask a question with regard to the testing of cattle for tuberculosis in the area immediately surrounding Kingston. I do not see him in his place at the moment, but I understand, from the records which I have looked up since he spoke to me, that the township of Pittsburgh, immediately outside of Kingston, is pronounced clear until April, 1946. I am not in a position to state whether immediately after April we can go on with testing, but it is high up in the list of counties and townships to be tested again just as early as possible.
Are any new areas being tested at the moment for restricted areas?

Those being tested for the first time are the districts of Algoma and Cochrane in Ontario, the district of Church-bridge and the municipality of Grant in Saskatchewan, being No. 372, and Camrose, No. 427 in Alberta. Thus it would appear that there are two in Ontario, two in Saskatchewan and one in Alberta which have been tested recently.
What are the prospects for enlarging this work in the near future? I understand that there has been a let-down during the war years. Several people want to organize now to carry on.

Our main problem is staff. At the present time we are spending all the money on this that we have staff to make use of. We are hoping we shall have more staff as we get further beyond the war period. I know quite a number of men who were available at one time have been serving in other capacities during the war, and we may have them back. If so we can do more of this work.

I know the minister is anxious to get through his estimates, but the hon. member for Brant, who was called away to-day, had prepared an excellent address on the health of animals branch. If the minister should not get through all his estimates to-day would he allow the hon. member to reopen that subject later?

My understanding is that the supplementaries have not yet been brought down, and there will almost certainly be an item in the supplementaries in regard to contagious diseases, on which he could bring up that matter.

A programme was in effect last year and perhaps before that of vaccination for the prevention of Bang's disease. What progress is being made in that regard?
tMr. Gardiner.]
It is still being carried on in the same way as it was a year ago. Does the hon. member want the statistics in regard to it?
I should just like to know whether it is proving successful.

Yes, it is proving reasonably successful. The story told the other night by the hon. member for Lanark I think illustrated very well the usefulness of the method in tending to eradicate Bang's disease, and we are having much the same experience with it.
Has the department experimented with streptomycin for Bang's disease? If so, has it been indicated that this drug will cure Bang's disease as well as shipping fever?
