19.	Plant products-seeds, feeds, fertilizers, insecticides and fungicides control, including grant of $18,900 to Canadian Seed Growers Association, $601,294.

Can the minister give some indication of the supply situation with regard to clover seeds and other small seeds this year, and whether there will be any restrictions on the export of these seeds? Have we available more than we shall need in Canada? What is the situation?

The supply of seeds this year is low as compared with other years. We are short of alsike and red clover; we have some alfalfa for export but nothing like what we have had in some previous years. The supply of seeds is down.
Will there be restrictions on exports?

I should like to ask about the supply of fertilizer, and whether any experiments have been conducted to find out whether artificial or chemical fertilizers have any detrimental effects on the land on which they are used. In my part of the country quite a lot of this fertilizer is being used and some people now have the idea that it is detrimental to the land. If it is, we should know something about it. If it is not, we shall be able to give the answer to some of these rumours.

Canadian production of fertilizers, particularly nitrogen and phosphoric acid fertilizers, is still going on at full capacity of the plants, and as a result the united nations, through the combined food board, are obtaining hundreds of thousands of tons of ammonium sulphate, ammonium nitrate, ammonium phosphate and cyanimide for allocation to the many countries, particularly in liberated Europe, which require them for the production of food. That is, our production is sufficiently high to enable us to export considerable quantities of these fertilizers to countries that need them. The supply of fertilizers for Canadian use is allocated by the combined food and materials boards of the united nations. These boards have a fertilizer committee with headquarters at Washington, and the administrator is the Canadian representative on that committee. The boards have allocated to Canada sufficient fertilizers of the various kinds for the entire Canadian demand next spring, provided
that the demand does not again increase substantially. That is, they have provided for some increase, but if there is a great increase there may not be as much as is required. The consumption of fertilizers in Canada has increased from approximately 300,000 tons in 1940 to 650,000 tons in the calendar year 1945, or more than double. Despite this, however, we have been fortunate in obtaining an increased supply to meet the increased demand.
In reply to the other part of the question, my information is that in any of our experimental work it has not been found that these fertilizers do any particular harm. Probably the effectiveness of the fertilizer in producing results is somewhat dependent upon weather conditions.

I realize that unless we have plenty of moisture one is further ahead to leave the fertilizer in the sack. If no experiments have been conducted so far, could that not be done, in order to find out if they have any detrimental effect?
Are any fertilizer chemicals being exported other than ammonium nitrate?

In the statement I
have just made I said the Canadian production of fertilizers, particularly nitrogen and phosphoric acid fertilizers, is still going on at the full capacity of the plants, and as a result the united nations, through the combined food board, are obtaining hundreds of thousands of tons of ammonium sulphate, ammonium nitrate, ammonium phosphate and cyanimide for allocation to the many countries, particularly in liberated Europe, which require them for the production of food.
Are export permits required for the export of clover seeds and other small seeds this year?
Yes, they are required, and they are all being handled through the special products board.

I should like to ask the minister a question or two in regard to this seed situation, which is a serious one. The account that was given yesterday of the deliberations of the dominion-provincial agricultural conference shows that the production of grass seeds, particularly alfalfa and red clover, has been very much lower this year than in former years. We do not want to be left in the position, particularly in eastern Canada, of running short of these seeds, because there will be a very heavy demand for them next spring. On previous occasions measures have had to be taken to see that enough was
Supply-Agriculture

retained in Canada to supply the needs of the eastern market. Alfalfa particularly is in short supply in Ontario. The farmers will need a great deal of it for seed and we shall have to depend to a great extent upon western production. The same is true of red clover, though not to the same extent. Are any measures being taken to see that a sufficient supply is being kept in the Canadian market? I would ask the minister to tell us whether the export board with headquarters at Lindsay has made any contracts for the shipment of seed overseas for the British authorities.

At the conference which was held earlier in the week we suggested that there should be a material increase. From 7,450,000 pounds we are asking for 15,000,000 pounds this year, or more than double the quantity. That is not altogether under the control of the farmers, because weather has a great deal to do with it. We are paying freight on alfalfa seed from Winnipeg to eastern Canada in order to encourage the shipment of seed from Winnipeg to the east rather than from Winnipeg south, the object being to retain as much seed as possible in Canada.

I have figures to show that in 1944, production in Canada was 9i million pounds. Last year, 1945, it was only million pounds, which would indicate that this coming spring there will be a shortage of seed for seeding purposes.
There is a shortage.

We want to be assured in eastern Canada that we shall have sufficient seed, because many of the meadows have been killed and there will be a large amount of land sown to grass seed in the spring. Measures should be taken to see that Ontario and Quebec will have sufficient seed. I do not think there will be any difficulty about the price, because Ontario will pay as good a price for the seed they need as can be obtained for export seed. Some provision should be made, before exports take place to any great extent, to see to it that Ontario and eastern Canada generally have a proper supply.

The matter of export has been under control all season and still is. It is impossible to export any of it unless a permit is obtained, and that permit is issued only where it is essential that the seed should be exported. The effort is to keep seed in Canada, and we are assisting in shipping it from Winnipeg east to make sure that it will come to this part of the country.

Has the export board any price set for seed for export purposes up to the moment? They generally have.
[Mr Senn.]
For 99 per cent, purity,. 90 per cent germination seed, it is 33 cents at. Winnipeg.
Has the government taken action, on the recommendation of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, with respect to the Calgary plant for the production of fertilizer?

The plant at Calgary produces ammonium nitrate. It has been operated as one of three plants during the war, the product having been utilized largely for the production of explosives and things of the kind. Representations were made by the farm federation to the effect that this plant ought to be taken over by the government and operated to produce fertilizer now that the war is over. The plant has been operated by the Department of Munitions and Supply. But my understanding is that of the three plants, the one that will probably be operated as a government plant is most likely to be the one in the eastern part of Canada in the Niagara peninsula, for certain reasons which have to do with supplies that are to be provided to some of the allied countries having something still to do with munitions. There has been however a tendency to consider the policy of disposing of the plant at Calgary. The question whether it should be disposed of to some private concern or to a farm cooperative or some other organization of the kind is under consideration. I am informed that the department has no set views in the matter. If the farmers' cooperative desires to have the plant operated, or if it can make arrangements to that end, its wishes will be facilitated. However, that is under discussion and there is nothing more I can say about it.

20.	Grants to fairs -and exhibitions, in the amounts detailed in the estimates, $62,690.

These grants, I believe, are made in part for the purpose of encouraging the improvement of live stock throughout the country, and in furtherance of that policy many of the associations hold race meetings during the time of the annual fairs. Included on the race programmes are events for Canadian-bred colts and fillies. It is necessary for a Canadian-bred colt in order to run in these races to be registered with the New York jockey club because we have no Canadian stud book for Canadian-bred horses. During this session we have discussed such questions as a Canadian flag for Canada and a nationality bill for Canadian citizens. Would the minister give consideration to a

Supply-Agriculture
Canadian stud book so that Canadian, colts may run by right on the tracks of the land in which they were born?

It is the intention of the department to promote the breeding of horses of the type mentioned, and we intend to get some stallions and have them placed under clubs. I understand that the department obtains stallions and puts them out to the clubs and the clubs pay for them over a period of years. The last part of the question, having to do with the registration of horses in New York in order that they may run on tracks, is another matter. We do register colts here the same as any other live stock is registered in the records branch, but the question whether they will be permitted to run on tracks is one that I cannot answer. It is pretty much under the control of those who operate the racing clubs and of the breeders. I am not too sure that there is much I can do about it. As a matter of fact the department does not directly operate the records branch. We simply give a grant to the records people and they record all the animals that are bred, whether they are dogs, cattle, pigs or whatever they may be. They have done such a good job of it up to date that we have hesitated to interfere.
What will be the policy of the government with regard to grants to classes A and B fairs during 1946?

I am speaking from memory, but I think during the first war we started giving grants to A and B fairs, and possibly some others, with certain ideas in mind. In between the two wars there was always a great deal of discussion as to whether we ever should have started them. It was argued by many people that the money could have been used to better advantage in some other way, but we continued to make the grants and entered into arrangements or understandings with the provinces from time to time. Sometimes we designated a certain class of fair as being one which would receive a certain class of grant, while others were left to the counties or the provinces to encourage.
Early in the war we struck off practically all grants that were paid by the Department of Agriculture except those to boys and girls clubs. We have under consideration in the preparation of our estimates for the next session the question whether they should be reestablished. Within the last month we have had delegations here from the different organizations that are represented suggesting that we should continue the grants. We have said to each of them that the question would be
given the fullest possible consideration between now and the time the estimates for next year are completed.

I should like to add my voice to the voices of those who have already made representations that these grants should be continued. I think they should be extended if possible. The minister will agree that our A and B fairs, as well as some of the smaller ones, have been of great assistance in improving the quality of our live stock and grains and other farm products. I know that some people take advantage of them and consider that they are simply a place to spend a holiday to see the side shows and all that, but the people who are really the salt of the earth, if I may use the expression, take great pride in their fairs and use them as a method of improving the quality of our farm products
Is it expected that the Ottawa and Toronto exhibition grounds will be available for fairs in 1946?
I have no information as to that; they are still occupied by troops.

What are the plans with respect to the maritime winter fair at Amherst? There is a vote of $5,000 to cover improvements, which is contributed to by the three maritime provinces. It is generally expected that the maritime winter fair will be reopened in 1946. I think the minister should make some announcement of policy so that the interested people may have as much notice as possible.

I believe the hon. member is referring to the agreement that we entered into some years ago with the organization that runs that fair. We agreed to pay $5,000 for building purposes, and each year we have been paj'ing that, even right through the war. We will continue to pay it until the agreement is completed. There is no suggestion that those grants will be discontinued. This is the type of grant that is made to fairs right across Canada by way of agreement. We have been carrying out those agreements and will continue to do so.

If it is proposed to reestablish the maritime winter fair in 1946 there will have to be a grant in next year's estimates for the purpose. Can the minister give any indication as to what policy will be followed?

That is what we were discussing a few moments ago. Communications have been received from the Toronto winter fair and other fairs across Canada, as well as the exhibition associations, asking what we have in mind. I have told them
Supply-Agriculture

practically what I told the committee a few moments ago, namely, that the policy we followed prior to the war had been set up after negotiation with the provinces and that some understandings had been reached between ourselves and the provinces. At the moment we are having a dominion-provincial conference at which the collection and expenditure of revenues are being discussed. Until that gets a little further along I do not think we are in a position to announce a definite policy for the future. The policy is being worked out, and all those who are interested are keeping a close touch with us in regard to it. It will be made known at the earliest possible day.

I understand that the maritime stockbreeder's association wants this maritime winter fair reopened in 1946 and are making representations accordingly. I think it is desirable that a declaration of policy be made as early as possible.

During the noon recess I picked up a book on agriculture and was surprised to find that the first agricultural and cattle exhibition in America was held at New Amsterdam, United States of America, on October 14, 1641. That is just over three hundred years ago, sixteen years after the settlement of Manhattan.

Before the war the federal Department of Agriculture made a substantial grant to the Lachute fair, but during the war this grant was discontinued for the reasons just given by the minister. The Lachute fair is acknowledged to be one of the best in eastern Canada. I should like the minister to consider the resumption of that pre-war grant in 1946.
The Lachute fair received a grant because it was in the appropriate classification. If grants are paid under any policy that is announced in the future, this fair will receive its grant.

The minister has referred to classes A and B fairs as being those in receipt of federal government grants. There has been a certain amount of agitation to get grants for fairs not in those categories. Will the minister tell the committee just what is a class A or class B fair? I think it depends somewhat on the amount of the prizes given, but I am not sure.

They were classified
according to the amount of live stock showing that was done, the attendance, and all that kind of thing. The class A fairs would

cover such fairs as Toronto, which is the greatest of them all, and the one at Vancouver and-
Ottawa?

Yes. There is a group of fairs in the A classification, and then there is another group in the B classification. I could get the whole list, but I think those who live in the communities know pretty well what they are.

There are a number of fairs that feel that the larger fairs in A or B classes do not need grants to the same extent that the smaller fairs do. These smaller fairs are doing good work throughout the country. I was just trying to find out what would put a fair in a class lower than B and thus bar it from a government grant.

They were based on the amount of prize money paid. I quite agree that it might be true that the larger the fair, the less it needs assistance. But there is another side to the picture. The more localized a fair is, the less is the argument that assistance should come from the federal treasury. In some places the assistance comes from the county, and in other places it comes .from the provinces; then there are those fairs where it comes from the dominion. In some cases assistance is given by both the dominion and the province. These things will all have to be worked out in the arrangement between the provinces and the federal government and our grants will be made where they will be the most effective.

Marketing service-
22. Marketing service administration, $111,742.

May I ask what steps are being taken to continue and enlarge our market for eggs in Great Britain? As the minister knows, but perhaps many members do not, the egg and poultry industry of British Columbia has greatly increased, so much so that this fall the largest shipment of eggs that ever left the shores of Canada left the port of New Westminister-294 million British Columbia eggs in one shipment. That is 24 million cases, or seven eggs for every man, woman and child in Great Britain. The poultry keepers of British Columbia are wondering -what is going to happen when that great British market begins to be supplied from the continent of Europe. They have built up their plants in British Columbia, and although they realize that a market is assured in Britain for 1945 and perhaps half of 1946, they would

Supply-Agriculture
like to know what steps are being taken by the department to cover the period following the end of the agreement.

I had all the egg statistics with me the other night and put some of them on Hansard. I do not seem to be able to put my hands on them now. I can only repeat what I said the other night. Prior to the war we were marketing about 1,000,000 dozen of eggs in Britain each year. This last year we marketed 85,000,000 dozen; in other words the increase has been 85 times during that period. I do not know that it can be claimed that that would have happened in any event, even if the government had done nothing about it, but the government did try to promote agreements with the British government for the purchase of eggs right from the beginning of the war, and we were able to bring about an increase in their purchases. Then, too, we developed in cooperation with the British and others the process of dehydrating eggs, which allowed us to ship over seven times as much by weight of eggs in a given space in dried form as we could in the shell. That was at a time when it was essential that we should get out shipments into as small a space and down to as small a weight as possible. So a large portion of the shipments that we have made, as indicated by the figures I put on Hansard the other night, was due to the dehydration process which was developed and which made possible the shipment of eggs in powdered form.
There was also a process developed for which British Columbia is entitled to the credit-the dipping of eggs in oil, a process I do not fully understand. By the use of that process it is possible for eggs to be kept fresh for a long period of time. At the beginning of the war these eggs were classified as storage eggs. We were insistent at that time that they should be classified as fresh eggs when shipped from this country to Great Britain, and now these eggs are accepted as fresh by Britain as a result of our experience during the war. This British Columbia process of supplying eggs in the oil-dipped form has resulted in a greatly increased shipment of what are now known as fresh eggs to the European market, particularly Britain. That in itself will bring higher returns to Canadian egg producers right across the country, the classification of these eggs as fresh rather than as storage eggs.

When these estimates were before the committee yesterday I brought to the attention of the minister two cases of what we considered discrimination. The minister dealt with one case, but I did not get an answer in respect to the other. My
question was, why could not the farmer who raises hogs and wants to feed his own grain to them get the same bonus as the man who buys his feed for hogs?
There is another matter I want to bring to the minister's attention, and it has been brought to his attention many times in the last few years. For a long time the farmers of this country have not been satisfied with the methods of marketing live stock. Through their different organizations they have on many occasions asked the government to set up a live stock commission for the handling of live stock. I want to put on Hansard a statement that was issued by the United Farmers of Canada in September last in connection with the selling of live stock. It reads as follows:
Live stock producers are entirely at the mercy of the packer buyer, who has sole command of the only market for live stock disposal in Canada, and the price for live animals is whatever the packer buyer chooses to make it, whether in the packer's yard or the packer's drover agent on the producer's farm or ranch.
Previously the producer had at least four main markets for his cattle:
(1)	The feeder buyers in his own or neighbour provinces;
(2)	The eastern feeder buyer;
(3)	The American feeder buyer and market;
(4)	The Canadian packing companies.
Numbers one and two markets are gone
through owing to the feed situation and policy uncertainty. Number three is closed. Number four therefore is in supreme command, and as they are in control of a market with competition almost entirely eliminated, and as there are no floor or ceiling prices on live animals producers must take their price whether delivered individually, through a drover, through a commission firm or by their own cooperatives, which can only benefit them by reducing assembling costs.
On the other hand packers have two -inexhaustible markets at their disposal with fixed prices; first, the domestic market for which they receive -the wholesale ceiling price, which is widely different to the price -received by producers; second, the Canadian meat board, which agency will buy any volume of beef from -the packers at fixed prices based on grades.
Producers will only get fair prices when animals are in -short supply but never above the packer's ceiling price; then when the flow of cattle becomes heavy the -purchase price paid to producers has been -and will again be below the packer's fixed floor price.
The government has a multitude of -live stock -and meat boards and committees with little policy cohesion, and -the chasm between the man who ra-ises the animal and all others engaged in the service -and in the industry is as wide -as the seas.
During the past few years, great strides have been made to improve -and increase the industry of animal production in Canada, and producers have hitherto been very patient, but they now feel -that their industry has been kicked around enough and that perhaps official -advisers and those with an assured profit in the industry could for a change start producing -and determine their own profits.

In another debate in the house this session, a member of this group, urging the government to set up a board of live-stock commissioners, quoted from a brief presented to the government by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in February, 1944, as follows:
This federation desires to repeat its request of former years that the federal government should establish a board of live-stock commissioners, with powers and duties similar to those of the board of grain commissioners. It requests that the said board be empowered to administer under the Department of Agriculture, the Live Stock and Livestock Products Act, and that the members of the board shall be appointed in consultation with organized agriculture. The Live Stock and Livestock Products Act should be amended and consolidated with other legislation in order to vest in the board the power to license, regulate, and control the facilities for assembling, transporting, yarding, slaughtering, processing, and packing, together with the facilities for grading and selling all live stock and carcass products designed for human consumption.
I think that shows defiinitely, Mr. Chairman, that the government should really take into consideration again this matter of a board of live stock commissioners. I notice that the minister in another statement in this house suggested that there were obstacles in the way, but I think that these obstacles should be overcome; he can find a way of getting around them.

About thirty-five years ago
I heard a student at Manitoba university by the name of James Gardiner debate the question of free trade. He upheld the negative side, and he won by a splendid margin. I congratulate him upon his statement at the recent agricultural conference here. It shows that he is still in favour of free trade, with the United States at least, so that he is growing in wisdom and in practical usefulness. Free trade should run north and south just as well as east and west. We should tell the United States government that we are not only practical neighbours as far as friendship is concerned, but real neighbours as far as tariffs are concerned. It should work both ways-not one thing for the United States and another thing for Canada; let us show the world that we are real neighbours.

You would put every
factory in Port Arthur out of business.

I have no hesitation in supporting my Irish friend and former Irish neighbour across the floor. I have on many previous occasions brought up the question of guaranteed prices for producers of live stock, and again I must appeal to the minister to do something in the way of giving that guarantee to the producer. As has been shown on many

occasions, the markets fluctuate, and these fluctuations are all to the benefit of the packers at the expense of the producers. It was shown, I think, that in October last the packers had a margin of about two and a half dollars on each hog shipped, and all that was at the expense of the producers. It is about time something was done to protect the producer against the fluctuation of the markets.

Are there any regulations
in regard to the inspection of peaches which are shipped to market. I understand that the only regulations are as to size, and that there are none as to the condition of the peach, as to how green it is. This has been the trouble with the marketing of peaches during the last five or six years, and perhaps longer. The peach must reach a certain stage before it will ripen after it has been shipped. Despite the fact that shippers have little tags in their baskets which say, "When these peaches are received in your home, spread them out on something flat so that they will ripen," during the last five or six years green peaches have been shipped which would never ripen, and the Canadian consumer has been fooled; there is no doubt of that. Now there must be a remedy, and I understand that that remedy is for the minister's department to put iu the proper inspection at the shipping point, and also see to it that all fruit is inspected which is taken away from the peach orchards. A great deal can be said for this, and I believe the real peach grower would be thankful if the government would do- something in that regard.

When we were considering the publicity and extension division I endeavoured to bring up the matter of advertising of Canadian dairy products in Great Britain. I referred not only to advertising but to making our products available to the British public in a form which would be suitable to them. Will the minister explain just how our cheese is marketed in Great Britain? It is my understanding that between the two wars New Zealand captured a great deal of the Canadian market for cheese in Great Britain. My information is this was largely because she made her cheese available to the British
REVISE!) EDITION
Supply-Agriculture

market. She had cold storage plants there where the cheese can ripen and be available at all times. Have we such cold storage plants in Great Britain? What is our policy with respect to the marketing of our cheese and the maintenance of the market which we now *have? It is very important to a large section of our dairy industry that we should retain that market, and we can do so only by having supplies always available there in the form in which the British public want them, rather than having them available only at certain seasons of the year.

The suggestion that the New Zealand people did capture a considerable part of the British market between the two wars, is, of course, in accordance with the facts. We were heavy producers of cheese which was required in the British market, and we were sending it to that market prior to the last war and during the war. But at the end of the war we took the attitude, which some people seem inclined to take at the end of this war, that our product had a certain value and we would not sell it for any less. The result was that the British began buying New Zealand cheese in greater and greater quantities.
As I remember the story, the New Zealand people accepted the price for their cheese which they were offered, and produced1 it in large quantities and sent it over. It is true that they did have facilities to handle it, but they did more than that; they advertised it thoroughly, so that by 1936, when I had my first experience with it personally, they had made great strides. I was over in Britain discussing the possibilities of greater marketing of farm products, and everywhere one looked he saw New Zealand cheese advertised, but in 1936 Canadian cheese was not advertised anywhere. As one walked out on the Strand from the Savoy hotel and looked about half a mile down the street where the street had been widened and there is a building extending out across the sidewalk, he saw on the top of that building: "Eat New Zealand Cheese". More people walk that half mile going to Work every morning and two or three times a day than any other half mile in the world. This sign was in front of them all the time, but nothing about Canadian cheese, nothing about Canadian products of any kind. The same situation was true of the buses. Every bus that passed you on the street had a sign on it reading: "Eat New Zealand Cheese", and nothing about Canadian cheese. I came back to Canada and sent six men over to Britain to look into the matter, and then I asked them to get out a pamphlet. After I got that pamphlet out I remember I had considerable
	.
trouble, not with the people in Canada, not with the people in Britain, but with some people in the house; with the result that probably it was not as widely circulated as it should have been. Nevertheless it said just what my hon. friend has been suggesting in the last few moments. It said that our cheese and other farm products were not being advertised in Britain, and it proposed ways and means of getting that advertising.
In the years between that time and the war, Canadian farm products were greatly advertised. It was not done under the agricultural department direct; it was done under the Department of Trade and Commerce and in a measure through external affairs. But it was done, and we came into the war with much more of our Canadian cheese on the British market than we had in 1935 and 1936. During the war we have gone on pushing first the production and then the 'marketing of cheese in Great Britain, with the result that in 1942 we obtained the largest production we ever had in the history of Canada. We got up to over 200 million pounds, and we sent 140 odd million pounds to Britain. We are in a favourable position at this time.
I quite agree that one of the things we have to continue to do, now that the war is over, is advertise our product in Britain. We have before the government at the present time consideration of a policy of extending our facilities for the handling of not only cheese but other products on the other side, as New Zealand has done. It has been suggested in the first place that we should improve our cold storage facilities on the wharves in this country; that we should improve our cold storage shipping facilities on the railways across Canada, and thus put our product on board ships in good condition. We should improve our refrigeration facilities on boats going across to the other side, and then we believe we should have some facilities on the other side for the proper storage of Canadian bacon, cheese, and other food of the kind that we are sending over, in order to maintain them in a reasonably good condition until they are placed on the market in Britain.
I quite agree that the suggestion which has been made is one to which we should give some thought, and that is being done at the present time.

Could the minister give us some idea as to the government's policy of continuing the bonus on cheese? This is important to the cheese industry, as they say it takes a year from the time of planning to the time of marketing. I notice in the estimates that the total bonus paid on cheese last year

was not equivalent to the bonus on apples. It does not seem to me that that comparison is a favourable one for the cheese industry.

The premium that we pay on cheese was, of course, being paid before the war started. It continued through the war and so far as I know will continue indefinitely. We pay a premium on 93 and 94 score cheese, and that we shall continue to pay. That is the only direct subsidy we pay on cheese. At the present time we pay a subsidy on milk which enters into the production of cheese, which is much the same thing as paying it directly on cheese. Of course that subsidy will be considered when we are making any change from the policy now carried out under the War Measures Act to the policy which may be carried out under the floors prices legislation. At the moment I. am not in a position to say what the nature of it will be, but the endeavour during the transitional period will be to maintain the relationship between the price of cheese and the prices of the commodities the producer of cheese has to buy, as has been stated here on a number of occasions. In addition one must keep in mind the fact that we have a contract with Britain which will continue until the spring of 1947 and fvhich guarantees the present floor price of cheese for that period of time. The premium is on as well, and the only thing we are not absolutely assured of is the milk subsidy. So far as I know that will be retained for some time, but I do not know just how long.

I should like to emphasize that point, because I think the minister will appreciate the fact that cheese production is an important matter in Canada and of great concern to war-torn Europe and to Britain. However, to enable farmers engaged in the *manufacture of cheese to produce the quantity and quality desired, considerable guidance must be given before the cheese production season comes along, so that they can plan in advance how to dispose of their milk, whether to the cheese factories, the dairies, or the creameries. In other years we have criticized the minister for being a little late in giving the farmers the information they require, and if we could get these directions earlier than we have been able to get them in past years it would be of interest and benefit to the farmers and to the country as a whole.

I should like to ask the minister just what standing our cheese has in Great Britain, so far as quality goes, as compared with New Zealand cheese, for instance.
Mr. .GARDINER: Our cheese has been right at the top of the list so far as quality is

concerned. That is indicated by the fact that we have always enjoyed a premium of two or three cents a pound as compared with New Zealand cheese, and that was so even before the war. Our cheese is recognized as being right at the top in the matter of giving the quality they require in Britain.

Yesterday I called the
minister's attention to a protest from the New Brunswick cheese producers' association in reference to the regulation of the board of health which requires that, cheese mature for a period of ninety days. At that time I understood there was not very much that could be done in that connection, though I think it is a serious threat to the cheese industry in our province. In New Brunswick they seem to like their cheese quite green, and they sell principally to their local market. Personally I have not acquired a taste for green cheese, but this is a serious matter down there. One of the great difficulties we shall encounter if this regulation remains in force is in connection with storage facilities in the small cheese factories. I believe the larger factories are given a subsidy for the construction of storage space, but in the small cheese factories no such provision is made. I should like to know whether some arrangement could not be made for tjie storage of cheese at some central place. The town of Sussex in my constituency is the centre of the cheese industry; as a matter of fact I believe about eighty per cent of the cheese factories in the province are-in Kings and Queens counties, which fornt the constituency of Royal. I believe these-cheese producers will be in a serious position unless something is done. A few minutes ago the minister spoke about storage facilities having been constructed across Canada, I should like to know if it would not be possible to provide some storage facilities in the town of Sussex. We have them now in Saint John and also in Moncton, but they are not sufficient to accommodate our cheese production if it has to be held for ninety days.
Of course we do assist those who are putting up storage facilities, in New Brunswick or wherever it may be, to the extent of thirty per cent of the cost.
That is in connection with the factory itself?

No, not the factory. There are two provisions. There is the old act, which I think has been in existence since at least 1922, which provides that wherever storage facilities are built, whether by a cooperative, an individual, a corporation or whoever it may be, and that cold storage is
Supply-Agriculture

available to the public, we pay thirty per cent of the cost. One-half that thirty per cent is paid in the year in which the plant is built, and the other half is spread over four years. That provision is available to anyone anywhere in Canada who puts up any storage facilities. Then under the act we passed in 1939, at the time we put a premium on the production of high quality cheese of 94 and 93 score, we agreed to pay for the cost of putting cold storage facilities right in the plant where .the cheese is made, in order to assist them in raising the standard of their cheese. We are doing that right across the country, too.
As to the other question having to do with the curing of cheese, speaking subject to correction because I am not too certain of our legal position in the matter, I think matters of health are largely under the control of the provinces. If the product is to be shipped out of the province of course it comes under our control and we can check the shipment of it. We brought in the regulation as the result of an epidemic of typhoid which broke out in Alberta, where the germ was traced back to a carrier who was providing milk for the production of cheese at a certain plant. Curing the cheese for a period of ninety days kills that germ, so it was stated that cheese had to be cured for ninety days as protection against the spread of typhoid. If those facts are correct I think everyone will agree that this is the thing which should be done.
To come back to the point raised by the ion. member, however, so far as we are *concerned I should think we could only enforce that in connection with the cheese that as shipped out. If the people of New Brunswick want to eat green cheese and things of the kind I am not too sure we could do much about it under tha.t regulation. It is only when we have the full cooperation of the provincial authorities, as I think we have had up to the moment, that we can enforce the regulation both provineially and inter-provincially. I would hesitate to suggest that we could change the regulation. Certainly I should not want to do so without very strong representations from all the provinces.

I quite agree with the
minister from the point of view of health, but I was asking about the cold storage facilities. Do I understand that 30 per cent of the cost is paid by the government if the cold storage facilities are maintained in the factory?
Then if the New Brunswick cheese producers' association set up a cold storage plant of their own the government would provide 30 per cent of the cost?
Yes.

Is there not some
chemical that could be used in cheese to kill the germ mentioned by the minister, without having to. cure it for ninety days?

I am not too sure whether there is such a chemical, but this is considered to be the simplest way of doing it. As a matter of fact I think it is one of the strong arguments for eating cheese, that curing it in this way makes it safer.

26. Fruit, vegetable aud maple products and honey, including grant of $5,000 to Canadian horticultural council, $567,000.

I was speaking before under vote 22 and I was told to bring up under this item the question of inspection of peaches. I understand that at present the peaches are inspected or graded only as to size. As I said before, I understand that the peach must reach a certain stage of maturity if it is to ripen after it has been shipped. Has the minister any suggestions to make, or could he tell us what they are doing along that line? I am quite sure the peach growers would welcome a proper type of inspection, because at present peaches that have not reached the proper stage of maturity when they are shipped do not ripen when received by the consumer; they rot and they are a total loss to the person who buys them.

I do not want to appear to be passing the buck to the provinces in connection with this matter; I am simply stating the facts. The grading of farm produce of different kinds, whether it is fruit or any other commodity, comes under the provincial authorities if the product is sold and marketed inside the province. We have no legal authority over that whatsoever. In so far as peaches are concerned, the grades would be established under the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act, which is a federal act. Those grades are reenacted under the provincial legislation. In the case of Ontario this .is the farm produce grading and sales act, which covers provincial enforcement. They have an act and we have an act. We have set up certain grades and certain qualifications and they have reenacted them. In most instances they employ our inspectors; they say that our inspectors are their inspectors in order to legalize the acts of our inspectors. When our inspectors are working within the province in connection with business carried on inside the province they are working under the provincial legislation, not under ours.
I think the situation in Ontario this last year was created largely by weather conditions. It was probably most difficult to supply the market there was for peaches with the highest grade of peaches. I think it is perfectly right to say that last year a great many peaches went on to the market which were supposed to be up to grade but which were not up to grade. I do not know to what extent such peaches got outside the province, but I have had no complaints from persons outside Ontario with regard to peaches that they obtained from Ontario. But I have had a lot of complaints about peaches sold in Ontario. Whether it was our inspector or the

provincial inspector who made the inspection, the inspection would be made under the provincial law. As I understand it, their grading would be just as high as ours and the inspected peaches would be the same whether marketed inside or outside the province, but because of the difficulties which occurred, much closer attention will be paid to grading and marketing during the coming year.

I have had reports of peaches that went into Quebec which were not ripe but which rotted in the bottom of the basket. I understand that there have also been complaints from Quebec with regard to the pink or red gauze put on top of the baskets. This pink gauze is put on top of green peaches, and it makes them look as though they are ripe and the purchaser buys them with that understanding. The department should have some regulation governing the grading. I do not think the minister has answered my question in regard to the grading as to greenness or quality. As I understand it, they are graded now only as to size. The dominion government is the agency that should see that they are graded properly. When a basket of peaches is marketed as being grade 1, it should be grade 1, instead of being a basket full of hard, green rocks.

I think that question
arises from the definition of "mature." The act states that unless otherwise defined, "mature" shall mean fruit that has reached the stage of development which ensures the completion of the ripening process. Probably that term will have to be more clearly defined before we can meet the situation.
That is exactly what I was trying to get at.

It has been assumed
that when one picks a peach or any other fruit it will be picked at that stage of ripeness which will ensure that in a reasonable time it will ripen, or by the time the cook comes to use it. I think it was found this year that the fruit was picked a little too green and it rotted very quickly. This caused a great deal of trouble right across the country. But as I say, that definition seems to be the source of the trouble and probably we shall have to try to make it tighter.	[DOT]

We are being asked to
vote a little over half a million dollars under this item. I have no objection to that, but I should like the minister to throw some light on a little problem that I have had brought to my attention on several occasions by correspondents in the southern part of my

Supply-Agriculture
constituency. This has to do with the marketing of perishable fruits by British Columbia growers outside that province. When I received this inquiry I went to the hon. member for Yale who helped me out. I remembered that he had been in the government when the Natural Products Marketing Act was first passed. The minister knows that that act was sent to the courts and declared to be ultra vires; it was taken to the privy council and they supported the decision of the courts. But that does not explain the position to the people who are interested. People in southern Alberta, and perhaps in other parts of the country, are unable to purchase fruit from an individual grower at a cheaper price, and some individual growers do not understand why they cannot sell outside the province and receive a little better price. The grower would get a better price and the consumer would have to pay less. I am not asking for a lengthy statement, but I wonder if the minister could take a minute or two to explain this problem.

This question has been
discussed. I think every year since I have been here, and I do not know that we have been able to get very far with it. Many years ago the provincial government of British Columbia passed a marketing act which gave authority to the organizations which control fruit in British Columbia to hold fruit off the market under certain circumstances. Among other powers which I do not wish to discuss this afternoon, they were given the power to hold certain species of apples from the market until other species had been entirely marketed. They also set the dates on which the apples shall be shipped. I stated once before on the floor of the house that a man came into my hotel room in Regina once and said to me, "Why cannot I buy such and such a species of apple?" I said, "Can't you?" He said, "No, I have been into a number of stores and cannot buy an apple, and I finally bought a case of oranges." I said, "That was your own decision. What are you suggesting I should do about it?" There is nothing I know that we can do. It had been decided that those apples of a certain species would not be marketed until a certain date until other apples had been got out of the way. That had been decided in British Columbia and there was not much I could do about it. I said, in discussing this matter before, that later on it might have the effect-it did not have that effect during the war-of making people want to eat something else or go somewhere else for their apples. However, it is British Columbia legislation, and it has
gone to the privy council, where it was decided that the legislation was within the powers of the province to pass and enforce. It has been enforced there and as British Columbia has decided that it is in their own interests I would hesitate to criticize it.

To come back to travelling expenses, I find that the travelling expenses over-all amount to SI,170,709. I am not criticizing that total because I have no doubt that it can be justified, but it would appear that this is a substantial travelling department. Do they use motor cars or railway passes, or do they have to pay the regular fares?

The travelling expenses for this particular branch are $59,000, or ten per cent of its expenditure. Our expenditures here are a little over $10,000,000, and the hon. member said that the total travelling expenses were $1,170,709, or a little over ten per cent, which is the same proportion that $59,000 bears to the expenditure for this particular branch. So that the travelling expenses seem to run about the same'all through the department. I have not examined other departments to find out how our travelling expenses compare with theirs, but I would be surprised if ours were not higher. The reason is that we have to deal with the affairs of 750,000 farmers, and our inspectors have to go right out on the farms and into all the markets for their products of those 750,000 farms, into creameries and everything of that kind all across the country, so that I would be surprised if our travelling expenses are not higher than those of other departments because our administration could not be properly carried out if that were not so.

Is there any overlapping between the provincial and federal departments of agriculture in the matter of inspection? I have received a letter from a dairy in my town, and this is the complaint the writer makes:
We have twelve or fourteen inspectors calling on us at present, namely, local health inspector, provincial health inspector, provincial milk test inspector, provincial milk control board inspector, provincial producer's inspector, scale inspector, smoke inspector, excise tax inspector, income tax inspector, unemployment insurance inspector . . .
And so forth. That is what they have to go through, although I know that some of these inspectors do not come under this department. But is there not overlapping between federal, provincial and municipal inspections?

That list indicates that not very many of those inspectors were attached to the Department of Agriculture,
Supply-Agriculture

but we take the blame for our share. I repeat what I said a few moments ago, that there is a definite ararngement between the provinces and the federal government that all through these services, the dairy branch, the fruit branch and I think in every case, the same inspectors are used for both federal and provincial inspection. What they do is to appoint our man to do the inspections required by the provinces. We try to avoid overlapping. In fact, at each of our agricultural conferences that we have had in the past ten years that has been one of the outstanding questions, and it has been agreed that everything possible has been done to avoid overlapping in the inspection service.

You have a milk inspector, a cheese inspector and a butter inspector. I can see no reason why one man could not inspect all three products, instead of one man being sent around the first of the week and another man around the last of the week. Surely, if a man knows something about milk, he should know something about cheese and butter.

There are two sides to that. A specialist in cheese is not necessarily a specialist in butter, and in many cases you probably could not use the same man. Again, the big cheese producing area is from Inger-soll straight through to Three Rivers. Some butter is produced in that area too, but western Ontario is more of a butter-producing area than a cheese-producing area. There may be the occasional cheese factory in that area. A cheese specialist would only be competent to visit a small percentage of the plants in that area unless he was a butter expert too, and they do not necessarily come that way. One man specializes in cheese and another in butter, and you have to have a competent man to give a satisfactory inspection.

I should think one man would be competent to iuspeoi; Butter, cheese and milk. If you call in a doctor, he can deal with measles, mumps and other ailments, and surely to goodness a man can be trained to inspect butter, cheese and milk instead of one man being sent to inspect cheese, another butter and another, milk. The dairymen have enough to put up with without all these inspections.

We want a specialist when we are very sick. But apart from that, cheese and butter inspectors seldom meet in the same factory, although you will find that in the province of Quebec. It is not a case of two or three men dropping in to the same place but of two men dropping in to two different places.

The only complaint I have heard about inspections in my district is that the inspector, who cotoes from Belleville, goes to just one dairy in the Peterborough district and takes a sample of milk to see if there is enough cream in it or too much. Then he goes back to Belleville and checks it, and then comes back the next day. for another sample. Belleville is a long way off, seventy-five miles away.
Perhaps he thinks some man there is crooked and he tries to drop in unexpectedly.

You cannot beat a man at his own game, and I know the minister is right. He must know my little preamble ' almost by heart by this time.
What I was talking about was the horrible quality of the bacon products we have had to consume in this country, and with good reason, over the last five or six years; but one of the questions I wanted to ask the minister was, to what extent are we sacrificing quality in our home-consumed product in order to send the best to the British market? As I intimated before, perhaps we should not talk about the matter with any accent on

Supply-Agriculture
sacrifice, because our sacrifices have been infinitesimal in comparison with what the consumer overseas has put up with.
I was overseas just prior to the war, and I made it my business to look into this matter of Canadian bacon. I wonder now what percentage of our home-consumed bacon comes from sows, stags and, heavies. I know that to compete with Irish and Danish bacon we have to send our best over there. I was amazed, however, when one of my colleagues -I take it we are all colleagues here-on the-Conservative benches talked about our having to do something about the matter because the Danes were "stealing" the British market for bacon.
They certainly are.

Yes; I think it was the hon. gentleman who has just spoken who said that the Danes were stealing the British market for bacon. I would suggest to the hon. gentleman that the Danes are merely coming back into their own.
They are getting their own and ours too.

We never had the British market for bacon.
It is not only in proximity to the purchasers that the Danes and the Irish have the advantage. The minister said, perhaps yesterday, that you had to have grain to raise pigs. The minister also knows that the less proportion of grain in a pig's diet, the better pork you have and the faster you can make it. The Irish peasant who has only one pig feeds it on buttermilk, boiled potatoes and whatever small amount of grain he can get; he raises the best pork in the world, and raises it faster than it is raised any other place I know. The same is true to some extent of the small Danish farmer, because he uses a large proportion of tankage and skim milk which he has available from the fact that he goes in for dairy products.
Just before the war I looked somewhat into this matter of Canadian bacon in Belfast, and from the point of view of quality. I was interested to hear the minister say that Canadian cheese held a unique place on the British market. I am glad to hear that. He knows. But I found that Canadian bacon was occupying at that time a very poor fourth place on the British market. As a matter of fact, I may say, I was able to buy bacon over there sliced and ready for the table-strange to say, Canadian bacon-at fifteen cents a pound less than my wife was paying in the city of Saskatoon, for the same brand of bacon which was being cured just 100 miles from that city.
The Irish people do not like Canadian bacon. I must state that frankly. Many of them had not heard of it, and those who had did not like it because it did not fulfil their requirements. What is the trouble in that particular situation?
That brings me to the packers. If we are to go on eating the kind of stuff we have been eating-sows and stags and heavies -for the last five or six years here, I want to know that we are eating it to some purpose. That meat is as nourishing as the meat we send to Britain, so that when the minister sends it over he must have in mind not only the nourishment of the British people but, as our hon. friend would say, the capture of the British market and the holding of as much of the British market as we can hold in view of the better competition of the Danes, the Irish and the English farmers themselves. I should like to be sure that the packers are not now doing what they did six years ago, being quite careless and dilatory in the matter of filling their requirements for the British market. I found this, for instance. I found out that the British market likes what I would call short-cured bacon; I think the proper term is "mild cured" bacon. I do not know what we do with our bacon or what chemicals we put on it, but we certainly make it so that it will keep well, perhaps in order to keep it in the hot weather. The British do not like that sort of bacon; they like a mild cured bacon; and I would like to be assured-and I think I am, by something the minister said yesterday-that he is looking into the matter of increased cold storage facilities by which that bacon can be taken over in a greener or milder stage to fill the British requirements.
Another thing I discovered about British opinion of Canadian bacon was this, that they could not be sure of any uniformity when they got bacon. When they bought bacon from one Canadian packer they got bacon of a different cure than when they bought it from another Canadian packer. You know how conservative the British are in their tastes. When they want bacon of a certain kind they want bacon of that kind, and that is the only kind they will buy. It was astonishing to me to find that our bacon, which I had thought was pretty good, was, as I say, a very poor fourth on the British market. So that, if we are to make the sacrifice which we are making-and hon. gentlemen know that the quality of the bacon we, have been eating is something terrific; you cannot get decent bacon any more; I fancy we are eating
