about 80 per cent of the rough bacon here. I should like to know from the minister what the percentage is.
That is about all I have to say on that matter. I should like, however, to direct three questions to the minister. I might add that during the war we did not mind eating that sort of bacon. If we thought we were doing our British brethren any good we would eat that kind of bacon or eat no bacon at all; but now that the war is over, the British will not be willing to take anything we care to send, or at any rate not for long. Just now they are in a condition where they are glad to take any piece of "sow belly" they can get their hands on.
Boiling this down to three questions, I should like to ask: first, what proportion of the bacon available in our Canadian stores today is rough meat of the kind I have described; second, what precautions are the packers and the department taking to see that there are proper facilities for taking to Britain the kind of bacon the British people want to buy; third, in a matter which the minister touched on to-day, relating to cheese, have we a thorough scheme of advertising in an attempt to hold the British market for bacon which our hon. friend says is in the process of being stolen from us?

I will answer the last question first, with regard to advertising, while it is fresh in my mind. With regard to advertising, during the war it was illegal to advertise any food in Britain. Britain bought all the food, took possession of it whether it came in from the outside or was produced inside, and distributed it.
I am assuming-

I am telling what the facts are up to the moment. We were not permitted, neither were the Danes nor anyone else, to advertise. The food products belonged to the government and were distributed by the government. They did not permit anybody to advertise any particular product. They said that the people had to take what they could get.
With regard to the quality of the product, we have standardized the bacon during the war. The different packers are not permitted to make their own brand and send it to Britain; they must make bacon of a cure that is set, and that was established during the war. We hope to maintain it. Whether we shall have the authority to maintain it after the war is over is another question. I doubt very much that we shall have much opposition to maintaining it. We hope we shall be able to maintain the standard.

With regard to the quality of what we have been sending over during the war, that is one of the reasons why I am most anxious to get over to Britain at this time. There is still bacon there which was shipped over during the war period. The hon. member is quite correct in saying that we had a rather heavy cure on our bacon during the war'. We had to have that. In the first place, boats were irregular, and in the second place food had to be got to Britain and stored. Whether it was good policy as a rule to do that with bacon or not, it had to be put there in great quantities so that they could have it if there was a blockade. Therefore we had to put bacon over there which would keep. When they said they were going to have a ration for a certain period of time they wanted to know that it would be available before the announcement was made, and it required to be kept over a long period. Well, we were afraid of that condition at the end of the war, because stories started coming over that the Danish people were getting back into the market in Britain. They have not got back to any great extent yet, as one would expect, but they were getting back in a manner which would have done harm to this country. They started immediately to make their mild cure bacon, and send it to Britain. They did not need to advertise. As has just been said, the British people like that kind of bacon and all the Danish people needed to do was to put it there. We sent Mr. Pearsall over to Britain to go into that question immediately it started, and we got a definite understanding then that the Danish bacon which was put on the British market would be cured like our own, a heavy cure, so that it could be stored alongside our own as long as ours could be stored, and that the two bacons were going on to the market in the same way. In other words, we said that if the Danish bacon were to go on mild, then we had better start shipping ours over mild too, in which case it would have to be consumed immediately it got there. An arrangement was made, and I think it has been working out satisfactorily since, so that our bacon is cured in the same way as the Danish bacon, and they go on the market on the same basis.
As to what we can do in the future, I do not think we can maintain the position that the Danish people must always put thei! product on the market so that it will keep, just as long as our product. We start ours moving from Edmonton through to Halifax or to Montreal and we put it on a boat and ship it across the ocean. We are shipping our commodity in cars and at times along with other commodities. Foods take on taints perhaps quicker than anything else.

Supply-Agriculture
We have not the same facilities for loading it in the boats that they have over there. Then their boats just carry bacon. They are built to do nothing but carry bacon. They take it across the North sea to Britain and unload it into facilities which are properly prepared for it. Their commodity does not suffer any great changes in temperature from the time it is first turned into bacon until it arrives on the British market. We must do that as nearly as we possibly can, but we cannot eliminate the distance which exists between Edmonton and London as compared with the distance between Denmark and Britain. Therefore we shall be at a disadvantage to that extent.
When I was over there in 1940 I met a man who I think is as good an expert as one could hope to meet. He was living in Glasgow; he was in the business and was appointed as the Scottish representative of the food ministry to handle all the food which came to Scotland. He told me definitely, as I said in this house before, that he had been eating Danish bacon prior to the war and never hoped to eat anything else, but for three months up to that time he had been eating Canadian bacon and that he would never go back to the Danish. He considered that Canadian bacon was as good as, and probably a little better than, the Danish, and he was going to continue to eat it for the rest of his life. I have no doubt that many people have come to that decision.
One or two statements were made with regard to the product which I do' not think are borne out by the opinion of the experts. For example, it was said a moment ago that these rougher forms of bacon or cured meats were just as good from the point of view of feeding people, giving them what is necessary for their nourishment as the higher quality, or what we call the higher quality of product. One thing is self-evident, whether one is an expert or not. The kind of bacon which the Danish people supplied to Britain, and the kind we tried to supply is a strip of fat and a strip of lean, a strip of fat and a strip of lean. The kind of product that we have been eating in Canada during the war lacked that extra strip of lean. If it is oil you want you can buy lard for twelve cents a pound. You do not want to pay forty-five cents a pound for fat. What you are really paying forty-five cents a pound for is the properly cured lean that is in the meat, and that is where the real food value is. It was not the fault of the packer that this other product was on the market. As a matter of fact, the packer prefers to put the best quality he has on the market where most of his product naturally goes. There has been great 47696-200}
competition among packers. There are two groups of packers. There is one group which exports, and another group which does not. Early in the war they were in competition with one another to the extent that they would come here and ask us to pass legislation for one group, which, if passed, might put the other group out of business. We said: "No, ve will not do that kind of thing." but that xe would have regulations which would make it possible for both of them to carry on, but they must carry on in competition.
I think that was best illustrated to me one day when I was out in the constituency of Humboldt trying to prevent the present hon. member for Humboldt from coming here at all. I was not successful, and that was his good fortune; but I was in a certain hotel one day and I thought the hotel-keeper was not any too friendly. He was sort of shying off to one side. Finally I went out and was going to go across the street. He joined me. When I got out across the sidewalk he became a little more friendly, and when we got in the middle of the street he stopped me where nobody on either side could hear what we were saying. He said to me: "I am a good friend of yours; I am a good friend of the government." He said, "I would not risk ask-ng this question inside the hotel, which I am going to ask you right here in the middle of the street." He said: "W'e are getting nothing to put on our hqtel table now but bacon that is made out of sows"

sow-belly, as my hon. friend said a while ago. He said: "Do you know that?" I said, "Yes, I know that." He said: "Who is responsible for that?" I said: "We are responsible for it. We told the packers that they had to send all the other pork over to Britain, and if we want to eat what we call bacon in this country it must be made out of something else for the time being. We take the responsibility for that." He said, "All right; I will explain it in that way. I was afraid to explain it in that way before."
I am not afraid to make that explanation. I know that sometimes even on trains, where you expect to get the very best, you got a little three-cornered piece of what looked like bacon and was cured like bacon. I made some inquiries to find out where that came from, and I was told that it caine from the jowl of the pig, off the jaw, and did not come from where the bacon usually comes at all. But we were eating it; we were getting a certain amount of oil out of it and a certain amount of lean meat, which to some extent at least met our requirements. I quite agree we should not have to eat that sort of meat after we get a little farther away from the war; but I repeat what I said yesterday, which some news-
Supply-Agriculture

papers took to be a prophecy in connection with rationing, although I did not intend it in that way. All I said was that if we were to be able to supply Britain with as much meat as we did last year, we must have some restrictions on consumption in Canada. One of the restrictions we hadi some time ago meant that if we wanted to eat the same number of pounds of meat that we had been eating we would have to accept the things we were not sending to Britain. Some people conceived' ways and means of curing portions that were not previously made into bacon in such a way that they tasted something like bacon and perhaps gave the same service to a degree. But if that kind of thing is to be carried on, probably we shall need along with it what we had during the war, and that is a certain amount of control over the prices of the different cuts. I do not know how long we can continue that; but in any event our effort would be to get for Britain as high a quality and as great a quantity of bacon as we possibly can during at least the next twelve months, and at the same time we shall try to keep on our own market food sold in accordance with its real food value. That is about all I can say at the moment.

The minister did not answer my first question, although I think it can be answered in a few words. I am well aware that we were not advertising Canadian bacon during the war; for one reason, even if we had been permitted we did not have to, because the Danish bacon was going to Germany and the British had no other place from which to get bacon. My question was whether or not the minister was going to take steps now to advertise our good Canadian bacon, as he has told us he has made plans to advertise cheese. My first question, the one I asked in the beginning, was as to what proportion of the meat on our home market is this rough meat, such as the minister has described.

Last month we were sending ninety per cent of all the high-grade bacon and ham to Britain. That percentage changes from time to time. I think I said yesterday that in the period when the price went down we were sending ninety per cent of the high-grade bacon and ham to Britain, but that extended only over a short period.

In the legislature of British Columbia last March I brought to the attention of the provincial minister of agriculture the necessity for a better egg inspection system in the interior of that province. I pointed out that large quantities of ungraded eggs were being sold by the unorganized egg producers, and that something should be done

about the matter, although very little had been said during the war by the organized producers. At that time I was told that this matter should be brought to the attention of the federal government, that it came within their jurisdiction. Well, I am here now, asking the Minister of Agriculture what can be done in the near future to remedy this situation.

That matter was brought to the attention of the proper officials of the department, and they now have under consideration the matter of putting in a better inspection system in British Columbia.
Mr. TOWNLEY-SMITH: To come back to the meat business for a moment, we have heard a great deal about the profits which have been made by western farmers, particularly, in the raising of hogs. I have always regarded those profits with some suspicion, for in my own case they were rather nebulous. I have a letter from the council of Canadian meat packers containing a table of hog production costs headed, "Is hog production profitable at present prices?" I wonder if hon. members would be' interested in hearing the farmer's break-down of' some of these figures. I will accept them without argument, because there is not time to discuss them. At any rate they show that it costs $17.20 to feed a hog to the marketable stage. Up in my country last year the young pig, the weanling, was worth $5 when it was six weeks old. Some sold for a little more, some for a little less, but $5 was the average price. So that if we add $5 to 117.20 worth of feed we get a total of $22.20. According to the figures contained in this table, a grade B-l carcass-and most of our carcasses are B-l-is worth $28.40, which gives the farmer a leeway of $6.20 between what he receives for the carcass and the cost of the pig and the feed.
This $6.20 has to take care of various things, such as chopping the feed; the interest on the outlay for buildings; occasional losses, because even pigs occasionally die; the hauling of pigs to the market and the hauling of feed, as well as the labour. If we apply that amount of $6.20 to labour alone we find that it covers a period of four and a half months or eighteen weeks during which the pig has to be fed. If you divide 18 into $6.20 it works out to thirty-four cents a week, or roughly five cents per pig per day, and that has to tak care of all these things. However, since this form was printed the market has fallen by roughly $2 per animal, so that we have to revise our figures, and instead of having a leeway of $6.20 we have only $4.20. That works out at twenty-three cents a week or 3^ cents a day, to take care of labour,

Supply-Agriculture
chopping, outlay on buildings, occasional losses and hauling. Therefore, when the farmer comes in at night and breaks down this 3J cents under all these headings and figures out his income tax, he learns what profit he has made.

I have waited for a long time to reach this item; I have not tried to make this statement on something els,e so that I hope the minister will hear me now. What I have to say has to do with the price of hogs. I have a letter enclosing an article from the Western Producer of October 25 calling attention to the fact that immediately after the government announced that ninety per cent of all available bacon would be taken for export to Great Britain the price fell $1.25 per hundredweight. In order to explain this situation I wonder if the minister could tell me how the price for what we ship to Britain is set. I understood'-and I hope the minister will correct me if I am wrong-that the price paid the packers for overseas shipments is set by the meat board. If that is correct, will the minister explain what relation this price set for overseas shipments bears to the price which prevails in the domestic market, and how that price is arrived at. If the minister will answer that I will follow it up with another question.
I think I dealt with that the other day; probably the hon>. member was not here.
I looked through Hansard and saw a reference to quantities but not to prices.

The basis of the price the packer obtains is set not by the meat board but by an agreement entered into between the meat board and the British government. The meat board, acting for the Department of Agriculture here, enters into an agreement with officials of the food ministry in Great Britain that a certain price will be paid by the British food ministry for bacon, laid down at the port. They took delivery of it at the port and assumed all the risks from there on, getting it across the ocean. That has been the established policy during the war. The way in which that price has been set since 1940 is this. We went to Britain in 1940 and took the officials of the meat board with us, and we sat down with the food ministry in Britain and discussed the whole question, what they would require and what they could pay for it. At that time they said they would not pay more than eighty-one shillings per hundredweight for bacon laid down at Saint John. It would not have made any difference what we thought; we could
not get any other price. They said, "That is all we have to pay for it, and that is what it must be." We started from that basis. We said, "That price will result in our bacon going to the United States long before the end of this year." They replied, "We will deal with that situation when we come to it."
In May, 1941, our bacon would have gone to the United States, but the British government raised their price from eighty shillings to eighty-five shillings, and they intimated that that was the most they would be able to pay for the product during the war period. They said that if we were to give them bacon, the Canadian government would have to deal with any additional allowance that would have to be paid in order to keep it from going to the United States. That was before the United States came into the war.
We then paid as high as $3.50 per hundredweight in order to keep hogs in this country instead of having them go to the other side. When the price got up to that figure we came to the conclusion that we could no longer pay out of the treasury and therefore we placed an embargo on hogs going to the United States. We would not permit the export of hogs there at all. We took possession of the product and sent it to Britain. All I can say with regard to the price is that at eventually reached 113 shillings and we took care of it out of Mutual Aid. I would emphasize the fact that this statement of subsidies that we have here does not include things like that at all.
We have a list of subsidies paid on farm products running up to $258 million, but it does not include the amount of money taken out of Mutual Aid to make possible farm prices in Canada which we have experienced since the British came to the point where they could not pay more. That is true not only of bacon but of cheese and of nearly every* other product that we have shipped. Much of that amount is really subsidy taken out of the treasury and paid to the farmer to establish that price. That is the basis of the price, and that covers the part of the question asked as to whether this price was set by the meat board. That is the floor price. We buy everything anyone attempts to sell, at a lower price than that, in the way of bacon and ham, which is the greater part of the hogs; that establishes the floor price on hogs, and that price has never been below a reasonable variation between the price of hogs and the price of pork since the time we first entered into these agreements.
In addition to that, we have had a ceiling price since 1941. That is on pork products and not on hogs. In 1941, when we were

Supply-Agriculture
back at the stage where the price of bacon laid down was at the lower levels I have spoken of, there was a very wide margin between the floor and the ceiling, and every year we increased that floor upward until we got it last year to where the variation between floor and ceiling on hogs amounted to thirty cents. The only variation you could have between the ceiling and the floor was about thirty cents a hundred on hogs.
As has been suggested, last summer, for a while, there was a margin of $1.25 between what had been established as the floor before and what was actually the ceiling. In other words, there was somewhere around ninety cents which people found it difficult to explain. Most of that is explained by one of two factors, and it lasted for only a few weeks and therefore did not affect greatly what had been happening during the rest of the year.
There could be only one of two answers. One is that somebody was bidding against the packer who supplied the bacon for overseas, for hogs in order to get the pork for the home market where there was a demand for it, where they could sell it above the ceiling; and if that were true, then there was .a black market in Canada just as there was In the -United States in the same period. We :are not responsible for that; we tried to -prevent it as far as we could. On the other hand, people were asking for bacon at the * ceiling price. They were asking for pork products at the ceiling price; and the purchaser *of these products being a packer, if you like, whether of the type that ships to Britain or of the type that markets his product in Canada, was saying, "We have had certain customers for a period of time and we want to keep them." There was nothing that said that there should be a ceiling or a floor in respect of hogs. It was established by the policy being carried out. But there was a ceiling on pork. The assumption is that, unless people were breaking the law, some of those purchasing hogs did pay prices higher than would be reasonable, if the ceiling on pork controlled the price of hogs, and so they got it to $1.25 above where it had been previously.
As I said the other day, the explanation called for is not as to why it came down but as to why it went up. The price is now on the same level as it was in 1944, and if it is maintained on that level we cannot say that the packer or anyone else is breaking the law in relation to it. We believe that somebody got outside the regulations in the short period of two or three months when we all ate all we wanted in Canada.

The explanation given by the minister has done much to clear up the point, but it raises another question. If I understood the minister correctly, he said that the basic price is set by the price arrived at between his officials and Great Britain. They indicated to the meat board the price they would pay and that went up as high as 113 shillings a hundredweight.
- That is where it is now. It has been that way since February, 1944.

That was the basis -for
hog prices throughout Canada, and I believe the minister said that if anyone was quoting hogs at a lower price than that the department bought them at the equivalent of 113 shillings.

I had better make that clear. We were prepared at all times to buy all the bacon in Canada cured in inspected plants on that basis, and the hon. member will agree with me that no packer would sell it for less when we were prepared to buy it at that figure. That established the floor.
This is where a further explanation may clear up the point. I find that 85 shillings a hundredweight comes to $18.72 and 143 shillings comes to $24.75.

It is $22.50, to be
exact. I was speaking in terms of 112 pounds, which is the British hundredweight, and that makes a difference. The actual figure is $22.50.

Can the minister explain how that is related to the figures, quoted on the markets here for grade B, which is the general run, of $18.06 in September-which was the high for this fall-and $17.33, which was the low for this fall? That low followed the announcement that 90 per cent of all production would be used for overseas, and the producer cannot understand why, when the government takes hogs for overseas shipment at the comparatively high price the minister has disclosed, there should be a sudden drop immediately after the government announces that 90 per cent of all bacon produced would be sold at that price.

Ninety per cent of the bacon is not ninety per cent of the hog. That bacon is made out of what are known as Wiltshire sides. You lop off the head and the feet and trim off a lot of other meat, and then what is left is called the Wiltshire side. You would require to have figures on all the different cuts that do not go into the Wiltshire side and what they were sold at.

Supply-Agriculture

This article in the Western Producer states:
Two weeks back, the meat board announced it would take ninety per cent of the hogs slaughtered at inspected plants (excepting sows and stags) for export to Britain. The prices paid producers by the packers immediately slumped $1.25 per hundredweight.
Not ninety per cent of the bacon, but ninety per cent of the hogs slaughtered.

I do not know what article the hon. member is quoting, but what was taken was ninety per cent of the A and B hogs. Those are the hogs from which we wish to take the British bacon. We took ninety per cent of them off the market for a period of time in order to supply that extra amount which was asked for by the ministry of food. It would be difficult to take it and apply it to the total marketing of hogs in Canada in order to figure it out. The annual marketing review of 1944 summarizes it over a four or five year period.

I still am unable to understand why that drop should take place in view of the fact that the price set, in accordance with the minister's figures, was very much higher than that which prevailed immediately after the announcement- was made. Immediately the announcement was made the price dropped, according to' the Department of Agriculture figures, by an average of seventy-three cents.

The fact is that the price dropped because it went up. It is another case of what goes up must come down. The price went up between May and August by exactly the amount my friend says dt came down. It started at a level between the floor and the ceiling for 1944 and the first four months of 1945. At the end of that time we said that we were not going to have rationing in Canada, that they could sell all the pork they like'd. Immediately those who were buying hogs started to pay more for them because they could sell them, not at the floor or not at the average but at the ceiling. Everybody in the business started buying hogs and selling them. There were no restrictions as to where they could sell them. A man would sell them out in the country to somebody who would bring them in to Toronto. During that period of time the price went up $1.25.
When we came back into the market again, in September I think it was, and said that we were going to have rationing, that we were going to have controls, these people could not sell hogs wherever they liked. They had to be graded under certain classes and this all
brought the price back to the level where it was before. As I say, at the end of the period it came down when these controls were put on again. Instead of selling most of our product in the home market at the ceiling, we were selling most of it at the floor in the British market.

I am not trying to be smart, but as far as I have been able to follow the minister's argument it would appear that the packers were getting away with something before he stepped into the market in September. That is the only explanation I can give for the fact that prices went up in the way that has just been described, and then came down again. Will the minister say whether that is correct?

I would say that by any figuring we have been able to do the packers must have been losing money for a few weeks. They were supplying us with meat at a price at which they could not supply it when they were paying those prices for hogs. As I tried to explain a while ago, a business man will sometimes do that when he knows the price will eventually come back. I have not been able to make some other people believe it, but I believe myself that the packers did lose money.

Possibly I should have made my remarks a little sooner, but I just wish to assure the Minister of Agriculture that the next time he feels like coming to Humboldt to give our people information similar to what he has been giving the committee this afternoon, we shall have a better place for him to meet us than the centre of the street. I was pleased with the success of my friends in smoking out these questions into the open even if that had to be done in the middle of the street.
For many years I have had an opportunity of discussing the bacon situation, both domestic and export, with friends of mine. Some of them were bom and raised in England, have been over here for many years but have gone back home for visits. Others still live in England. When I ask them what they think of the possibility of Canadian bacon taking first place on their market their answer invariably is, "You will have to send us different bacon from the shrivelled stuff you are sending now." They tell me that the bacon which comes from Canada is thin and not the type that they want. I believe the minister and many other hon. members realize that a hog which is properly fed will give better bacon at 250 pounds weight than it will at 200 pounds weight. Many of the experts disagree as to
Supply-Agriculture

that, but in my opinion I think a mistake has been made to emphasize getting thin hogs on to the market at too early a stage in their growth. I agree with the minister when he says that you do not want to pay forty-five cents a pound for fat or grease when you can buy lard at twelve or fourteen cents a pound, but I know that many a slice of bacon off a 200 pound hog has just as much or more fat than a slice of bacon from a 250 pound hog and there is not the same amount of lean meat.
I was wondering if the officials of the department could not help this situation by finding out what is the trouble. In my opinion the trouble is that we farmers, through force of circumstances, have been compelled to rush thin, young hogs to the market before they have reached their proper maturity and had got up to a certain weight. When those hogs are sent to the market you do not get the kind of bacon that the hon. member for Saskatoon City was calling for. I just wish to draw this matter to the attention of the minister. I know he cannot do anything about it now, but I think this is something that should be given consideration if we are to compete with the Danish people in the British market.
Our weights are exactly the same as the Danish weights. In order to compete we made our weights the same.
Is that all that is concerned in it?
No; they are right and we are right.

This is not just an isolated case. The British consumers of our product are complaining that they do not like the thin, shrivelled up stuff we are sending them. Denmark may have some system by which that weight is attained with a month or two added age. They would thus get a different type of meat.

Would the minister
explain why the bonus is not paid to the farmer who feeds his own grain?

First, I do not know of any way in which it could be done. I know of no way whatever in which you could prove to the auditors of the department that' a man had fed a particular amount of grain to a pig or a steer. But that is not the reason why the position is taken. We are paying a far higher subsidy on meat or dairy products that are produced from the feeding of the grain than we are paying on the grain itself over and above the basic price, not only through
\*ir. Burton.]
what we got out of Mutual Aid but through these other subsidies that were put on Hansard yesterday. That makes it not only unnecessary but. inadvisable to our mind to pay a subsidy on what is fed to the animal. We pay the subsidy on the animal itself. We pay the farmer to feed the grain to the hog. We do not want to pay him, on top of that, another subsidy on the grain that he is feeding to the hog. The man who buys the grain also gets the subsidy, but nearly all of them are in eastern Canada; and to that extent it may be true to say, as one member did the other day, that some advantage is probably being given to the eastern feeder. If there is a feeder near Winnipeg or Edmonton or anywhere else out there feeding grain to his hogs, we make some allowance on the grain just as well as to the prairie farmer on the grain he buys. We would have had a greater outcry than we have over this if we had not done that.
I still do not agree with the minister. The department knows to a pound how much grain it takes to feed a pig.
Nobody here will admit that we know because they are all asking whether it pays or not.
The fact remains that the farmer who feeds his own grain is under a handicap.

Since the matter of subsidies has been raised I wish to make myself clear lest what I said the other day be misinterpreted.
A subsidy is paid on grain to producers in western- Canada and a subsidy is paid on the freight to eastern Canada. I am not objecting to these subsidies either on the freight or on the grain produced in western Canada, but when wm start to pay subsidies we very often upset the balance between our economies in different parts of the country, and that is just what is taking place with respect to these subsidies. Take cattle, for instance. At the present time the government is paying the freight on feeder cattle brought from western Canada to eastern Canada. The government also pays the freight on the feed grain brought east to feed those cattle. It seems to me that you are giving an advantage to the feeder in the east in that respect unless you are prepared at the same time to pay the freight on the finished product, that is on the cattle fed in western Canada and then brought to eastern Canada. If you are paying these two subsidies, the price of cattle should be the same on the eastern and

Supply-Agriculture
western markets. There is no justification for the difference in that price when the production in the east is being subsidized.
I would ask the minister to take this matter into consideration, because it does place the western feeder and the man who has fed his cattle on the farm in western Canada in a different position from the man who has fed his own cattle on his farm in eastern Canada. I think they should both be on the same footing if we are to pay subsidies at all.

What we are doing' is dealing with a particular problem. We say to the farmer in Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes:	If you will go out into the
drought area and buy cattle direct from the farmer who has not the feed to feed them and bring them east, we will pay the freight. That is done just because there is a lack of feed in that area, and we limit it to that area. I have no hesitation in saying that we also help to pay for the feed that comes here to feed those cattle. We are dealing with a temporary problem that has to do with the drought area. We would not want to apply that principle to the cattle that come east.
I would ask the minister if there is a penalty on packers buying pork hogs below the ceiling price?
No.
No. Is there a penalty for selling pork above the ceiling price?
Yes.
There is no penalty for buying at low prices standard hogs on which a ceiling price is set?
There would be a penalty if the packing plant did not carry out that undertaking. We would not buy their bacon, and that would be the biggest penalty you could inflict.

I understand from farmers in my district that their prices fluctuate. If the packing house did buy below the floor price, is the only penalty on the packing house that you would not buy their product?
That is the only one I know of, but it is the biggest one you could inflict on them.

If a case of a packing house buying below the floor price is brought to the attention of the government, what would the penalty be? Would the government refuse to buy any of their products, or would it refuse to buy say just two sides of bacon?
Under the authority given to the meat board, to which some members of the house apparently were opposed the other night, the meat board can absolutely close up the packing plant?

The minister's memory must be better than mine as to what happened the other night, because everybody on this side was unanimous that controls on feed prices should be retained. There are other controls that were objected to, but no one objected to controls on food prices.

Item agreed to.
Marketing service

28. Marketing of agricultural products, including temporary appontments that may be required to be made, notwithstanding anything contained in the Civil Service Act, the amount available for such appointments not to exceed $15,000, $25,000.

The farmers are very anxious to know just what is going to happen to farm prices now that the war is over. They have not forgotten what happened after the last war when prices dropped so low that many farmers never recovered from their loss. The farmers want assurance that this will not happen again. The minister has encouraged increased production of farm products, and the farmers have done everything possible to comply with his request until agricultural production has practically doubled. Farmers now find their barns filled with live stock. There are more live stock on the farms to-day than ever before in the history of Canada.
Hogs, too?

Are we to have losses on a scale similar to" those we experienced after the last war? That is the question the farmers are asking to-day. I have a list here of the monthly average for the years immediately following the war. In June, 1920, the average price for good butcher steers was $15.02 a hundred; in November, 1921, that price had dropped to $5.57. That is, in less than a year and a half prices had fallen almost two-thirds. I consider that the farmers have a right to ask, are we to have a guarantee that this will not happen after this war? The only wajq in my opinion, that it can be prevented is by floors under farm products.
I was greatly surprised at an article which appeared on December 1 in the Ottawa Journal, the Toronto Globe and Mail, and other papers, reporting an interview with Hon. T. L. Kennedy, minister of agriculture of Ontario. I am not going to read all the article, but only a small portion of it. The heading is:
Will demand agricultural controls end.
Supply-Agriculture

It goes on:
Toronto, November 30-T. L. Kennedy, Ontario minister of agriculture, said to-day that he will demand immediate abolition of all war-time controls on Ontario agriculture when he appears next week before the agriculture committee set up by the dominion-provincial conference in Ottawa.
He said in an interview that the time had come to abolish price ceilings and price floors and let the farming industry find its own natural floor and ceiling.
That is, the minister says, in effect, "I don't want a guaranteed price on farm products; I want them to find their natural floors."
As1- I pointed out, that was the course of affairs after the last war. Prices found their natural floors, with a drop of almost two-thirds from the selling price during the war.
May I point out briefly what the government of Great Britain is doing in an effort to assist the farmers by guaranteeing prices for farm products. Mr. Williams, in the House . of Commons, said:
The government will establish assured markets and guaranteed prices for the principal agricultural products,-milk, fat live stock, eggs, cereals, potatoes, and sugar beet . . . The existing system of fixing prices for fat live stock, milk and eggs will be developed to cover the period after June, 1948, when the present guarantees would cease to operate. For these branches of food production, a new system of overlapping four-year periods with reviews will be established. Thus, in February, 1946, minimum prices will be established for the period ending June, 1950, and in 1948 prices for the period 1950 to 1952 will be set.
That is a guarantee price for seven years, to be continued from that time on.
There are some 20,000 applications for farm loans by returned men in 'the Dominion of Canada to-day. These young men who are buying farms are purchasing their stock and equipment at very high prices. According to Mr. Kennedy, if these prices are to find their floor in a natural way, how many of these soldiers will be able to pay for the farms they have bought? Surely these returned men. as well as other farmers, are entitled to some protection in the way of guaranteed prices.
I trust that the government and the Minister of Agriculture will pay no attention to the unwise and surely thoughtless demands of the Ontario minister of agriculture and that floor prices on farm products in Canada will be continued.

In reply to the hon. gentleman who was addressing the committee when we adjourned I wish to say that the Hon. Tom Kennedy, minister of agriculture of Ontario, is a practical farmer who enjoys the confidence of farmers in particular and, I think, of the people in general, and it is pretty hard to judge his remarks on the basis of a news report. I wish to make this statement for the benefit of my hon. friend.

What is to be the future of some of the specialized products of western

Supply-Agriculture
Ontario? We have some problems there which are peculiar to our district. First, I would refer to our beans. As the minister well knows, a ceiling was fixed on beans early in the war, and it was fixed too low. Then we were subsidized to the extent of fifty cents. Later we were granted a price for the domestic consumption on yre basis of participating certificates. The exportable surplus of our crop, which we had committed ourselves to send to Britain, was paid for at the rate of $3, and we have been settling our participation certificates at the rate of nineteen cents. This afternoon one hon. member referred to floor prices, and I would associate myself with the statement made by my colleague the hon. member for Grey North in regard to the remarks of the minister concerning ceilings, floors and controls. When these controls are taken away, what will be the future of the Ontario farmer?
For a moment I should like to deal with another problem which is very close to us in western Ontario; that is, the matter of tobacco. Certain controls were set up in 1933 under the Natural Products Marketing Act. When that act was discarded in 1935, the growers, who were well aware of the extent to which they had benefited under it, organized themselves on a purely voluntary basis, on which they have been carrying on ever since. The successful marketing of our product was due largely to our control measures. It is true that we had a small exportable surplus, but the greater part of our product was consumed in Canada. We had production control. That may or may not be popular with the minister, but in connection with some of our specialized products it is important to the primary producer. So that I should like' to ask the minister what is to be our future, since in order to cooperate with all the regulations which apparently were necessary during the war, and in order to make a contribution to the whole country, we willingly gave up the control measures under which we had been working. When these prices come back, with our controls taken away, what assurance shall we have that we shall be given certain protection in the years that lie ahead?
We have another problem as well, if I am not going too fast. I mentioned that we had suffered because of low ceilings. I have mentioned the fact that we gave up our production controls. Hon. members have listened to a great deal of talk about wheat, but there has not been a great deal of talk about Ontario wheat. The price of our wheat was frozen at a level at which it is not economically sound to produce it iD western Ontario.
We produce wheat for the straw, silly as that may sound. To-day that wheat is selling at $1.09, and it costs more than that to produce. What are we to do in the future? Must we come back to the government and ask for the reinstatement of the control policy, which was acceptable both to the companies and to the growers? I may be rambling from one product to the other, but these are problems which are very close to the farmers of western Ontario.
If I may come back to tobacco for a moment, as I have said we were willing and glad to give up our production control for the sake of the war effort; but we convinced the people of one thing. In nine years of operation we increased the price received by the producer by from seven to nine cents; we maintained the level of dividends to the shareholders of the company, and we did not increase the cost to the consumer by one iota. We thought that was quite an accomplishment. If this system is to be discarded; if the companies are not convinced and will not play ball with the primary producers, it is time that these matters were brought to the attention of the government, because we are coming into days that will be extremely competitive. We do not know exactly what Great Britain will do in the matter of preferential tariffs, and so on, so that I would ask the minister if there is any assurance that in future these specialized products will be protected.

The question raised by the statements just made is one that is vital to agriculture in this country. I think I should repeat what I said the other day to the conference of representatives of the nine provinces and the farm federation. I may be wrong, but I do not know of any line anywhere in the world more completely closed against the international marketing of products than is the Canadian-American boundary line against the marketing of farm products. During the war, because of restrictions which were found necessary in order to retain food in this country either for our own use or for the use of our allies, particularly Britain, we completely closed the United States boundary line. You just cannot ship anything out of this country into the United States. As against that, it can be said that if you were to open the boundary line to-morrow, with conditions as they are at present, inside of one week we would be pleading for food in every part of this country. The food would just disappear from this country within a week. It would go to the markets of the
Supply-Agriculture

United States and be sold there, unless we did something about our price levels as related to those in the United States.
In my opinion that is the present situation. I believe it is recognized by everyone that with beef prices, I think it is reasonable to say, three cents higher in the United States than they are here, and with prices of all other products similarly higher, if you were to open the market and let everybody ship their products to the United States, then food would just disappear .from this country. We would have great difficulty in maintaining enough food here to feed our own people. We probably could not do so. I think we are all agreed that that is a condition which could not continue very long. We have been listening to a discussion here for the last two or three days, and as Minister of Agriculture I have not had sufficient time to give adequate study to the question debated, but there are a few essential principles which I think apply at all times and some of these have been under discussion. I think it is obvious that we have to find something that will stabilize our values in the different countries at some early day. I am not prepared to say whether that should be the gold standard, or what it should be; but I think I have benefited sufficiently by the experiences of the last six years, when everything has been done by putting on controls of one kind or another to satisfy a particular group in some particular country for the time being in order to meet their own situation, to recognize that if we are ' to be afflicted now with that sort of thing after the war is over, if we are to go on without a regulator of some sort, there may be some danger ahead of us much more serious than even the gold standard. We might encounter some serious difficulties in getting back to the position to which we wish to revert in the .period of peace. At any rate that situation exists to-day, as far as agricultural products are concerned. There is a difference between the marketing of agricultural products in the United States now as compared with five years ago, a difference in values placed on everything as between one side of the line and the other, and beans is one of these commodities.
When my hon. friend and his delegation started to come here first to talk about marketing beans, the price of beans in Michigan was double what it was in this country, and if it had been possible to sell beans in the United States the price would have immediately gone up. But in the negotiations then going on to meet the situation in the United States and Britain we were asked to export our own beans and we went directly to

Britain and arranged a price. That price was satisfactory to the bean growers in western Ontario as long as they could buy what they wanted at the prices arranged for under present price controls, but it would not be satisfactory if they had to pay the same prices for what they wanted to buy as paid on the United States side of the line.
That is what we are talking about when we speak of the transitional period. That period will not come to an end until these questions are dealt with by somebody somewhere, and in the meantime it is my conviction that we have to maintain the position that exists in western Ontario and everywhere else at the expense of all the people of Canada until such time as we can get the situation adjusted to the place where we can trade as we used to trade and where we shall have values equalized on the two sides of an imaginary line such as exists from one coast to the other of this continent.
One can speak of relationships with Great Britain. There are other factors that operate there, and all these have to be adjusted. While they are being adjusted, we expect to apply the terms of what is generally known as the floor prices act passed in the last parliament preceding the election. We intend to see to it that the position of people such as the bean growers and others is safeguarded so long as it is necessary to safeguard it during the period when we are adjusting this condition which has been created by the war and for which the people themselves, who feel the effects of it, have had no direct responsibility.
The government^ all over the world have done the things they thought necessary to win the war, and now that the war is won we have to give consideration to these matters that have been brought to our attention by the hon. member whether they deal with special products or the products that we are producing in greater quantities and are being consumed. That is the intention of the act passed a year ago and the spirit of that act will be applied. We believe that if we apply it in that spirit we can maintain a relationship similar to that which has prevailed in the last two or three years.

Special-
29. Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and water storage, $2,000,000.

There is a question which I wish to ask the minister. It has reference to a serious situation in the Peace River block. If we were not so pressed for time, I would go into details, but I will content my-

Supply-Agriculture
self for the moment with reading a resolution I have received from the Peace River Improvement Association. It will bring the matter to the minister's attention, and I can then ask the question which I should like to have him answer. The resolution reads:
Whereas, farmers throughout 'Canada are being urged to produce the maximum of beef, pork, lamb and dairy products, and, whereas, the farmers of the British Columbia block of *the Peace River district have responded to the extent that in 1944 over one million dollars worth of live . stock were shipped from the block.
And, whereas the aforesaid farmers are anxious to maintain and increase that production.
And, whereas, this objective cannot be reached owing to the drastic shortage of water for stock and even for domestic use.
And, whereas, these farmers have been contributing to the P.F.R.A. since it was started.
And. whereas, the aforesaid farmers are financially unable to bear the entire costs of constructing stock-watering dams and dugouts.
And, whereas, people of this district have learned with considerable interest, of the very valuable work and assistance in this respect, given to farmers and ranchers of the prairie provinces,
Therefore, be it resolved that we, the members of the Peace River improvement association, respectfully urge the Hon. J. G. Gardiner, Minister of Agriculture for Canada, to make provisions of the P.F.R.A. Act applicable to the province of British Columbia, in order that farmers and ranchers in this province be afforded the very great advantages and benefits which could accrue to them from policies_ that are available under the act, with particular reference in our case to the plan of assistance in locating suitable sites for and in the construction of stock-watering dams and dugouts.
The question I wish to ask is this. Can the minister extend the benefits of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act beyond the limits of the Palliser triangle without further amendment to the act itself? If not, h^s he given consideration to the extension of the act beyond the prescribed limits or the application of it to all the provinces? Would the minister make a statement?

I think I can state in a few words what the present position is. As the name of the act indicates, it was intended only to deal with prairie farm rehabilitation. The act does not say definitely that it must be applied to the Palliser triangle, but it does suggest and the spirit of it is that it shall apply only to what is generally known as the drought area, and we try to confine it pretty much to the Palliser triangle. We were approached by all the provinces, and it certainly was recommended by a committee of the house during the last session that we should extend the principles of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act to all Canada. If
we were to do that, it would involve a material change in the responsibilities of the provinces in relation to a number of problems as compared with the responsibility of the federal government.
I think everything we are doing under the P.F.R.A. is, under our constitution, the responsibility of the provinces. The only reason that responsibility was accepted by the dominion when the act was first brought in in 1935, and when I brought in amendments in 1936 and 1937, was that we had induced people to go into an area that we knew to Ire exceptionally dry, and having induced them to go in we had a responsibility to reestablish them, now that the situation which we - had reason to expect at the beginning had been proved to be true. So we started out to reestablish them and we said that, irrespective of the fact that these were provincial obligations to people who had established themselves on land within the boundaries of the province, we would do. this particular thing.
If we are to assume new responsibilities in all the provinces, it seems to me that that question would be bound up in the larger question which is now being discussed at the dominion-provincial conference. It has been submitted to them and it is under discussion at the present time. If it is determined that there is to be a redistribution of funds and the sources from whi<:h funds come as between the provinces and the federal government, and that takes a certain direction, then I assume that we shall take on some of these obligations in a dominion-wide way. If that is done, then it would be quite reasonable to expect to extend the areas in the three western provinces into the north outside of what is generally known as the drought area, as well ' as to extend them into other parts of Canada.
I should like to make myself perfectly clear on that. I do not think an act such as the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act could be extended to ail Canada. Probably, if that policy were followed, we would have to have . the present Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act renamed and perhaps redrawn and apply it to the four western provinces. Then we would have to have another piece of legislation which would apply to the provisions east of the great lakes. I think the administration of works which would. be carried- on in western [DOT] Canada under a policy of that kind would have to be in western Canada, probably where it is now at Regina which is pretty central. We would then have to have another administration set up in eastern Canada to deal with eastern problems under a separate act.
I doubt if we could administer the whole

I am going to refer only to the last two words of the vote, "water storage." In doing this, I should like to lefer to an article which appeared recently in the Moose Jaw Times-Herald of September 17. which referred to an article which had appeared in the Regina Leader-Post of September 15. These articles refer to a serious condition that exists in connection with the water supply of Regina. The Moose Jaw Times-Herald, in referring to the proposal to build a dam on the Saskatchewan river which would permit the taking of water to Regina, says:
The project is a large one, and it ds not primarily proposed -as -a means of supplying the cities of Moose Jaw and Regina with -a visible and abundant water supply. The primary purpose is to provide water for irrigation of an immense acreage of farm -land -and the development of hydro electric power.
The article in the Regina Leader-Post of September 15 is headed, "City near limit of water supply," and reads:
Regina has pretty well reached the limit of her present water supply, J. W. D. Farrell, waterworks superintendent, said Friday.
Deep artesian wells from which the city has been taking its water give between 5,500,000 [DOT]and 6,000,000 gallons a day on the average. This summer the city could have used 7,000,000 gallons a day, if the quantity had been available.
What I have to say has to do with the water supply for these two cities. I have made a most extended survey into the problem as it affects these particular cities, and I maintain that the Dominion of Canada is responsible for this lack of water. I am not blaming the minister because I realize that he has done a job in solving problems, quite apart from the P.F.R.A. work to which I am not going to refer. An effort has been made during the last few years, I have no doubt under the minister's orders, to supply water to Moose Jaw. I think what has been done proves that water can be taken from the river to the city. During the past summer water was pumped over the bank of the river near Riverhurst to a total of 1,375 million gallons. But of that quantity only about 191 million gallons reached the Caron basin from which Moose Jaw draws its water. That showed a loss of the difference between 1,375 million gallons and 191 million gallons. This was due to the fact that an open ditch was used. I am not finding fault with that;
I am simply urging the minister, now that -it has been proved that water can be taken

from the river to Moose Jaw, to provide an adequate and proper system. That is what these two newspapers ask for in'their articles and I am going to support them.
They referred also to irrigation, but I am not going to touch on that problem tonight. However, I wish to say that I am in favour of irrigation between the river and Regina. I suppose before the dominion government could really enter into such an irrigation project there would have to be agreements with the three provinces that control the Saskatchewan river. This could be carried on under a Saskatchewan river authority. When the construction of Regina, and perhaps Moose Jaw, was first started, permission was given to take 100 cubic feet a second out of the Saskatchewan river, which is a much larger amount than these two cities are using to-day. As I said before, Regina is using at the moment about 5,500,000 gallons a day, and I presume Moose Jaw would use between 3,000,000 and 4,000,000 gallons a day, provided that they can get it, but that is not always the case. That would be less than twenty cubic feet a second, so that the original agreement entered into when these provinces were set up and which allowed 100 cubic feet a second would be ample.
I should like to see the minister bring in an item, not for $2,000,000 but for between $10,000,000 and $20,000,000. It should be at least $10,000,000, because to build a dam on the Saskatchewan river would cost $6,000,000 in any event, and perhaps a little more under present-day prices. I would suggest that if the minister does bring in a vote in another year to build a dam on the South Saskatchewan river, he keep before him a dam at that point which in the future could provide water for irrigation purposes for the district between the river and Regina, or right down to Este-van. The dam would be amply large enough to take, care of that, 'because the reservoir behind it would be approximately 75 to 100 miles long, and would conserve a large number of billions of tons of water. The water supply situation of Regina and Moose Jaw is serious. Regina is taking water from three different areas, from Boggy creek, from Mallory springs and from Mound- springs. Some time ago I read ani engineer's report which stated that by the constant drawing of water from those areas and the deepening of the artesian wells that receive supply from the whole prairie roundabout, the water plane of the whole prairie roundabout is being lowered. If that is true, it must have an effect on the farms roundabout. In my judgment, we should not delay in overcoming the lowering of the water plane, and I will support any

Supply-Agriculture
reasonable vote which the government brings in to relieve that situation. The sooner we commence, the better.
I would suggest to the minister that he bring in a vote that will be sufficient, first of all, to build the dam which the engineers say they have found a base for out there, and there is no trouble ini building a dam if you build the base wide enough, as they did on the Tennessee river. The dam should be built large enough not only to provide a reservoir of ample water for these cities for all time to come so long as the world lasts but to provide irrigation water if and when the proper body is set up to see that these irrigation works are carried out. It does not require a special body to be set up to construct a dam or to construct conduits from the dam to Moose Jaw and Regina. The department can do that itself through P.F.R.A., but legislation would likely have to be brought in to construct irrigation works between the river and Regina or right down to Estevan. I would urge first that we build the dam, and, second, construct conduits. The water would have to be pumped over the river bank. I would not recommend a dam 310 feet high at that point, because there would be too much pressure, but a dam 150 feet high could be constructed, and I would recommend that the water be carried in a conduit built of British Columbia cedar or pine; I forget just which is used in the building of conduits, but British Columbia timber is used in making irrigation conduits in that country. When British Columbia cedar is used the frost has no effect, but a conduit made of steel would be affected by frost.
As an easterner who in my business life profited greatly, not personally, but through the company with which I was associated and others, by the opening up of these cities in the west and through the effect which that had on the development of the prairies, I consider it my duty to urge the minister to bring in a vote for whatever amount is required to place these two cities on a proper foundation as far as their water supply for domestic purposes is concerned and as far as their water business requirements are concerned. See what happens to-day! The cost of the water for Moose Jaw, for instance, is much higher than it should be, through no fault of the department and no fault of Moose Jaw. If Moose Jaw and Regina could obtain water for domestic purposes at a low rate it would induce manufacturing concerns to establish themselves there; that would help to build up the west, and the more the west is built up through the development of cities, the
better it will be for all down here in the east. That is the doctrine I have preached right along, because I have been through it. I have seen how business has profited in the east and in the country generally through the opening up of the west, and I am convinced that if we could put these two cities on a proper basis as far as their domestic water supply is concerned their populations would be tripled and quadrupled in number as they should be, and that would help to develop the whole country.
I say to the minister: Do not hesitate; do not be too humble in asking for sufficient to do that job. Give these two cities a chance to live by supplying them with an ample water supply. If that is not done, the water plane all roundabout may go down and down and down, and that can all be prevented by bringing the water from the river.

Mr. Chairman, I have availed myself for several sessions of the opportunity offered by this vote to discuss particular problems in the maritime provinces. at the head of the bay of Fundy. I would refer to our marshlands. I do not believe that there has been in this house a proposal which has received such unanimous support and one about which so little has been done. I know that the minister himself has expressed his approval of framing a policy to deal with these marshlands, comprising from 100,000 to 150,000 acres which require protection from the sea, drainage, and tc be reclaimed. That word which we use so much in the post-war period, rehabilitation, certainly applies to this area. We have now arrived at the point where there should and must be some declaration of policy as to what is to be done with respect to this undertaking. Our people and the owners of the land want to know what is to be done, and it is certainly in the interests of the entire eastern part of Canada that there be a decision soon. We expect that it will be favourable.
Not only has the minister himself expressed his approval of the purposes and objectives of this undertaking but also the officials of his department, including the deputy minister, and the director of experimental farms, who comes from eastern Canada and who is so capable and understands the special problems in the east. These men have given it their approval. The director has authorized special development work and experiments at the experimental farm at Nappan. The superintendent is Mr. W. W. Baird, who has done special work in draining and cultivating this land, and with exceedingly satisfactory results,

securing three to four tons per acre of the very best hay for fodder purposes. Up to the present nothing has been done except to expend a few thousand dollars in conjunction with the provincial governments and the marsh owners in restoring breakages in the dykes. The Nova Scotia legislature has gone on record unanimously as favouring the reclamation of these lands. The New Brunswick legislature has done the ' same. Expremier the Hon. A. S. MacMillan, of Nova Scotia, .came to Ottawa and gave evidence before the committee on reconstruction and reestablishment. Hon. John A. McDonald, now Senator McDonald, who was minister of agriculture, came here and gave forceful evidence in this connection. Mr. McDonald was probably the most energetic minister of agriculture of any province in Canada. He never spared himself in advancing the interests of agriculture, and he strongly recommended action. The matter was dealt with before the committee on reconstruction and reestablishment in 1943, and a unanimous report was brought in recommending that something be done. That report, which was brought down to the house on January 26, 1944, and unanimously adopted, states that the committee has given a great deal of thought to the economic situation of the maritime provinces. It recommends that improvement be brought about "through assistance to the farming community, by the application of the provisions of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation- Act.'' The argument made before that committee was that with an expenditure annually of $2 million, aggregating up to the present time $20 million, valuable work had been done in the west, and that work should be done on these fertile marsh lands in the [DOT]east. That was the conclusion in a unanimous report of the committee, submitted to parliament and adopted unanimously.
We also have reports and recommendations from boards of trade and other public bodies, along the same lines. We had a visit by the leader of the Progressive Conservative party (Mr. Bracken). He made a thorough personal investigation of the conditions. He went down on the marsh to look through these aboideaux, and made inquiries, and examined the land. I am going to read from a statement made by him. Although I have not his authority to repeat it here, it is on record. The leader of the opposition said:
As a long-range policy, we propose to have the present Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act extended throughout -the farming areas of Canada, so -that it will become national in
(Mr. P. C. Black.]
scope. Just as drought areas are being reclaimed in western Canada, so, under a revised act, marshlands may be reclaimed from flooding in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
You have a big problem in the marshlands at the head of the bay of Fundy and other places, an area comprising some 150 thousand acres of marshlands . . . We propose, however, that the dominion share with the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick the cost of continuing -this reclamation.
Any present surveys should be reviewed; any necessary further surveys should be made at once. We shall share with the provinces the cost of such studies and we shall assist by generous financial aid the reclamation of these
A brief was submitted to the royal commission, known as the Dawson commission of Nova Scotia, from which I am going to read some recommendations. I do not say that these are final; I do not say that they should not be modified, but they constitute the basis of the representation made to the Dawson commission, and I understand that the commission reported favourably upon them, although I have not seen the report. The brief was presented on behalf of the agricultural society and on behalf of the board of trade of the town of Amherst; it had also the support of the board of trade of Sackville, the adjoining town. The chief requirements are:
(a)	The opening up of the main drainage rivers and canals, now blocked by sediment and vegetation. This is a machine job and should be done by the federal authorities.
(b)	Dykes and aboideaux should be built and strengthened. This was formerly done by hand labour, but now must be largely a machine operation and the federal government should assume considerable responsibility.
(c)	The main vent ditches -must be reopened and new ones dug. This too is now a machine job and might well be assisted by the provincial government.
(d)	Small drainage ditches- -must be dug wherever the marsh is cropped. The owners should have this responsibility but special ditching machines should be designed and supplied by the provincial government on a moderate rental basis.
(e)	A large supply of lime and some special fertilizer should be made available at low cost.
(f)	The land would in great part have to be ploughed and reseeded by the owners.
(g)	The marsh roadways require rebuilding and maintaining and the provincial government should assist in this work.
(h)	Marsh areas should be organized into as large bodies as possible, having natural boundaries and similar conditions. -
(i)	The more remote acreage in considerable sized blocks in different districts should be taken over by the government and improved for use as community pastures, such as has been done in the west.
These are general recommendations. I am not expecting that they will be adopted verbatim. They should be the basis upon

which a policy should be decided by the federal government with the cooperation of the provincial governments and in collaboration with the marsh owners, whereby this land would be reclaimed. It means not only the cropping of these fertile marshlands which grow three tons and more an acre of the best possible hay and clover and grain, but the building up of the uplands to the extent of two and three acres for every acre of marshland. Instead of retrogression, there would be development and prosperity where one finds nothing now but decay, a blot on the whole countryside. As to the amount of money which is asked for, and which I believe I can quote the minister as saying that he favours it is a very small amount in comparison with the sums we are voting at this time. A few days ago we voted $750 million in export credits in order that we may trade and assist other countries; and under the Bretton Woods agreement, which is still before the house, it is proposed to vote $300 million for an international monetary fund for world stabilization, and the establishment of an international bank for reconstruction and development-an additional amount of $325 million, plus United States exchange. So that the amount we ask for, $250,000 to $300,000 a year for that whole area at the head of the bay of Fundy, is a small 'amount in relation to the enormous expenditures being provided in this parliament, and in relation to the enormous amounts that we of the eastern provinces have supported and voted for under the prairie farm rehabilitation schemes since 1935. Up to the present time they have amounted to $20 millions. What the people at the head of the bay of Fundy, the provincial government, the municipalities and the marsh owners want is some declaration of policy, some prompt action in order that something may be done to enable them to know what to plan for. It is not something that can be done in a day or a year; it is a policy that should be put into effect and applied over a considerable period of time, so that the people in that whole area may gradually build up and reestablish what is one of the best stock raising centres in eastern Canada.
When we were dealing with the estimates of the Minister of National Defence, Army, I requested that some of the explosives which were being destroyed, because we have no further, use for them, be used in opening up some of these drainage ditches. Some of the newspapers did not take my suggestion seriously. I wrote to the department of agriculture in Washington and they sent me the United States department of agriculture
"Farmer's Bulletin, No. 1606." I shall quote a few sentences from that report. On page 5 we find the following:
While ditching with dynamite is possible under almost any conditions, it usually is economical only for making small ditches or cutoffs in stream channels, in soils other than gravel and dry sand. The most economical size of dynamite ditch is about three feet in depth and eight feet in top width; much larger ditches can be built in this manner but -the cost per cubic yard of excavation increases rapidly with the size. The ideal material for dynamite ditching is a saturated sedimentary soil that is firm but not as stiff as the hardest clays and is free from stumps and large roots.
The marshlands contain ideal soil in which to use this explosive for that purpose. I go on:
Many excellent ditches have been blasted under conditions quite different from these, but at increased cost. Where conditions are such that the work is adapted to any one of the several types of ditching machines, it generally is not advisable to use dynamite, but usually it is much cheaper to dig ditches with dynamite than with hand labour.
Then on page 6 we find the following:
The proper size and spacing of charges to give a clean-cut ditch of the desired depth must be determined experimentally for each set of conditions. This can best be done by firing a number of single charges, and when a size of charge is found which gives a smooth crater of the desired depth, a little less than the half diameter of the bottom of the crater will be the proper distance between charges . . . The proper distance between charges . . .
Then farther down:
The cost of ditch excavation by dynamite varies greatly. Under favourable conditions a pound of dynamite will blow out from one to two cubic yards of earth, making the cost for the explosive from fifteen to thirty cents per cubic yard. Very little labour is required for such ditching. A gang of four men will load and shoot about six hundred linear feet of singlerow charges per day. It is usually necessary to remove debris and smooth the sides and bottom of the ditch with shovels after blasting. This work should be done as soon as possible, and if done promptly should not cost more than one cent per linear foot of ditch. This method is very useful for straightening streams.
I am not going to say anything more except that we have enormous quantities of surplus explosives in this country. Much of this explosive must be destroyed. I ask the Minister of Agriculture and the department if they will not make an inquiry to see what can be done toward utilizing this waste explosive in opening up these drainage ditches on our marshland. I ask the minister and the department to announce their policy- I know he cannot do so now, but in the near future. For myself, I am going to support this vote to-night. I have supported it ever since I came to the house; but if something is not done in order to' do justice to eastern
