150,000	acres of the most fertile land in Canada, if I am here next session I shall move that the vote for the prairie farmers be reduced from $2,000,000, or whatever it is, to one dollar. I plead with the minister, the house and the government to take some action to announce some policy in conjunction with the provincial governments, and the marshland owners.

May I just say a word. To-night we have wandered from Peace river and the prairies down to the Atlantic coast. Everybody who has spoken has had a pretty good case to put before the Minister of . Agriculture in relation to water conservation or drainage. I suggest that when the next session comes around there should be a thorough discussion in this house or in the agriculture committee regarding the possibilities of water conservation, of irrigation and of drainage in various parts of Canada.
Some years ago in 1937 or 1938, I went into the problem of water conservation in Saskatchewan, and made a speech in this house which was criticized because it involved large sums of money, $30 or $40 millions as I remember it. I was glad to hear the hon. member for Davenport raising the problem of the utilization of the waters of the South Saskatchewan river and the use of that water not only for supplying the cities of Moose Jaw, and Regina with a good water supply- and I mean a softer water supply than Regina has-but for irrigating a large section of the country particularly south and east of the South Saskatchewan river.
When I was looking into the matter with a view to saying something in the house I remember that I had an opportunity of being shown by engineers the contours of the country from the place where the hon. member for Davenport suggests a dam should be built right down as far as Weyburn and Estevan. It was amazing to see that natural channels could be used for that water and the irrigation of a large section of Saskatchewan which I was told at that time could be done economically.
As far as the water of the cities is concerned, I had not seen this newspaper report from Regina. I know the condition in Moose Jaw. I happened to be on the city council when the last water supply was brought in from Mound springs. I think one of our dominion officials assured the council at that time that we were obtaining enough water then from Boggy creek and other sources for 125,000 people.

Before I sit down, may I just say to the hon. member for Cumberland, who has made the plea he always makes, and properly so, on behalf of the marshlands of the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, that I hope he will not suggest at any time that the amount appropriated for P.F.R.A. or any other project which is valuable to any section of Canada should be reduced. We remember, of course, that the two maritime provinces mentioned have received very considerable subsidies over a period of years for coal freight rates and other things, and we never objected to that because we believed it to be in the interests of the economy of Canada or we would not have supported it. And because we believe this water conservation proposal is in the interests of Canada we are prepared to support it and to urge it in this parliament. I am suggesting to the minister that at the next session the experts in his department and those in the Department of Mines and Resources, where I believe there are some persons interested in conservation, perhaps together with some of the young men who have done a great deal of investigation into the soils of western Canada and their probable productivity if properly supplied with water, be brought before the committee and we try to formulate, in cooperation with the government and then in support of a government policy, a water conservation policy for western Canada and a policy of reclaiming the marshes of the maritime provinces, so that we may

I am sorry to be so much in agreement with the leader of the C.C.F. party and to-be even so slightly in disagreement with the hon. member for Davenport, whom I and all the other people in western Canada believe to be the eastern statesman most sympathetic toward our part of the country; and I hope he heard me use the word "statesman" rather than "politician." We have heard a great deal about supplying Regina and Moose Jaw with water. I was in Regina when they got their first water supply; my father was mayor of that town, as it was then. The first wells were drilled at Boggy creek, six or seven miles to the east. We were rather worried about ourselves for a number of years, because they were drilled on a farm belonging to a Mrs. King. The people of Moose Jaw, who were jealous of us because they had no water then, said that we in Regina were drinking Mrs. King's water, and that is how the thing came about.
This scheme to bring water from the Saskatchewan river at a point near Riverhurst is not new, but I am going to make a suggestion to those people who want this government to spend that money. If the government appropriates money to give the cities of Regina and Moose Jaw a water supply, why should they not do the same for any city, town or village in Canada that requires it? I say this in the interests of the minister, because there are differences in jurisdiction. If we are to centralize everything here, then let us vote the money, which after all is the money of other people since not much of it belongs to us; let us vote it and do all these things, but let us realize that there must be a limit somewhere to government spending. I wish I could think of something in my own constituency for which I could ask the minister. I see the hon. member for Lethbridge almost glaring at me now, but we are rather a perfect constituency and do not need anything. You see, we kind of look after ourselves rather well. That, of course, is an exaggeration.
We have heard a great deal in this house about irrigation, [DOT] I am all for it; let there be no misunderstanding about that, but let us take the history of irrigation in western Canada. It begins and ends largely, I think, in the province of Alberta. The Canadian Pacific Railway company began it. They spent their money and had two districts, the
eastern district, which is the Brooks area, and the western district, which centres on the towns of Strathmore and Gleichen, just east of the city of Calgary. What has happened? They did their best with it; their engineers did an excellent job; but about eight or ten years ago the Canadian Pacific Railway company were very glad to give to what we now know as the eastern irrigation district everything they owned: ditches, houses, machinery and land, the whole works and $400,000 in cash to help them carry on. It is true that it is well operated and getting well on its feet, and this is the reason. While the farmers in that area would not pay the C.P.R., the directors of that show see to it now that everybody pays his water rates and taxes, so that it is a successful show.
Keep on a bit to the west and you come to the western block of that district. What happened? I was before the committee of the whole in the Alberta legislature, I think within the past year. What is happening there? Again the C.P.R. are giving to a newly formed district the whole works, everything they own, together with an amount in cash. I cannot remember the exact figure, but in any event it is somewhere between $300,000 and $400,000.
We speak of irrigating from the Saskatchewan river through Regina and Moose Jaw down to the Weybum and Estevah area. I have no doubt the slope of land is there, or the engineers could not have found it. But take that western block. Not five per cent of those persons who originally paid water rates are paying them now. Why? Because they do not need the water. The rains came, and that has been a prosperous area. So that within the past year, with Mr. Brownlee in the lead, what have they done? They had to go to the government to have this thing formed. There were certain persons who had paid their water rental and who, for the lifetime of their contracts, which was almost forever, wanted to make the C.P.R. supply them with water. So they had to go to the provincial legislature and the C.P.R. were relieved of their contracts with those very few people who were using that water.
We will go to the Lethbridge northern, if you like. Water was laid on there and it is a splendid area; and you can take the one out of Medicine Hat running down south of the Bow river; I think it was the Canada Land and Irrigation. Take those four projects; we all know they went broke and have been carrying on with assistance from here and there.

Do not tKink I am arguing against irrigation. I am not, but I know that if a man is going to work an irrigated farm he will have to work harder than I ever did or than I hope I ever shall. When a man makes a success of an irrigated farm you know you have a really hard-working man on that job. It is not easy to handle a six-foot shovel, with rubber boots, in mud up to your knees, keeping those ditches open, with a load of mud on your shovel to start with, trying to get one foot up and cleaned off so that you can get out another shovelful. That is what working in an irrigated farm means. I am all for irrigation, but neither this government nor any other government in Canada should go into this business on the basis of any minimum cost. The four projects I have named all came to grief. They are doing infinitely better now; they are on their feet, but if we are to spend money to build that dam on the river which the hon. member for Davenport has been seeking for so long, let us not go in on a two-dollar basis. If we are going to go into this thing, let us not go in on a two-dollar basis. It is a sixty-four dollar question. Do not let us make it lower than that. May I ask who is in charge of P.F.R.A. and what his salary is?
Mr. George Spence is in charge in\western Canada and his salary is 86,000.
Where is Mr. Gray?
He is under Mr. Spence handling the water part of it and he gets $4,500.

The remarks I have to make on this item will be brief, since previous speakers have covered a good deal of the territory I had previously planned to. discuss. I agree with the Minister of Agriculture when he says that the prairie areas are the areas in which the P.F.R.A. should have commenced, this being the diy section of Canada and the place where people have been settled, so that it rightly fell to the government to see that they were given some security against crop failure. I wish to assure hon. members from the maritimes who -have spoken that we in this group are not attempting to keep corralled for our own particular use anything that is good for all the people of Canada. I believe the marshlands project which one hon. member has described, is, from the small amount of study I have made of the subject, certainly a thing the government should consider.

In my opinion the whole of the P.F.R.A. might be lumped into one title, or one project, namely land utilization. I believe the P.F.R.A. is attempting to direct settlement to and use of land to the extent that it will have its optimum use. In some areas that might be land under forest crop; in other areas it might be land under grass; still in other areas it might be land under rotation; and in other areas again, as in southwestern Saskatchewan, it should probablj' be alternate crop and summer fallow.
P.F.R.A. has been lumped under three divisions. One is cultural work. Under the cultural work division- are formed the agricultural improvement associations. The agricultural improvement associations are an organization of farmers working together, thinking out their own problems, and at the same time they are given technical leadership by agricultural men both in the Department of Agriculture and in the universities. In our own particular area agricultural improvement association work has been directed mainly against the prevention of soil drifting, and with the help that farmers have been given through their associations they have gone a long way toward the control of soil drifting. The agricultural improvement associations are something that could be extended to all Canada, and I suggest that the minister should take that into consideration.
Under the land utilization part of prairie farm rehabilitation come the community pastures. I would suggest that P.F.R.A. be given some cash for buying land from farmers who hold title to land in areas which are perhaps to be formed into community pastures. I have seen the situation, and no doubt the minister has -seen dozens of them, in which one particular farmer does not want to leave his land; a fence is put around it, he stays in the community pasture and his neighbours are gone. It is an expense to P.F.R.A. So that P.F.R.A. should have a sum of money for the purpose of purchasing land from people who do not wish' to leave areas that are made into community pastures, or alternately the money should be used for the purpose of buying good farms which in turn can be traded to owners of land that is to be used as community pasture.
We have heard a good deal to-night about water development, and the main emphasis has been on large irrigation -works. I do not minimize the necessity for and the value that comes from large irrigation development, but I feel that if there is to be only a small amount of money devoted to P.F.R.A. it should be used almost entirely for small water development.

I believe"! am correct in saying that the amount of money P.F.R.A. to-day pays for a small dug-out is $125. In our area a number of dug-outs were built this year. Into that area came men with proper machinery and they would construct the farmer a dug-out which cost him $250. He could obtain $125 from P.F.R.A. There was crop failure in that area this year, and there are many farmers who need dug-outs but who have not the extra $125 to pay the contractor to build the dug-out. I would ask the minister if he is taking into consideration the question of increasing the amount that will be paid for small dug-outs. The small dug-out, of course, can provide farmers in that area an assured supply of water, both for home use and for the use of live stock. The farmers then, by having the dug-out, can keep increased numbers of live stock and obtain the benefits that come from diyersified farming.
It is estimated by Mr. George Spence, the P.F.R.A. director, that there could be engineered from 5,000 to 7,500 small water developments each year for a period of ten years. He estimates that the cost of that programme would be three-quarters of a million dollars each year. I would strongly urge the minister, while he has not seen fit to increase the amount allotted to P.F.R.A. this session, that he certainly increase it by much larger amounts next session.
A small irrigation project can give the farmer an assured supply of vegetables. If the farmer can irrigate an acre or two he can have a good garden and perhaps a small orchard. More than that, if he has any number of acres irrigated he is assured of adequate supplies of feed. P.Fit.A. officials estimate that an acre of irrigated land will stabilize fifteen to twenty acres of land. In other words, in the dry areas of Saskatchewan a farmer can grow enough feed on an acre of irrigated land to carry through the winter the live stock that he can pasture in the summer on fifteen to twenty acres of land. I believe the advantages of small irrigation developments are even greater than those I have mentioned. It would reduce to a considerable extent the present trend toward larger farms. If we can arrest that trend and maintain a denser population in our agricultural communities, it will mean better community life, better social services, better recreational facilities, better health services and, all in all; a much better life for our farmers.
I contend that the money which would be spent on small irrigation developments would be self-liquidating. We all know what happened in the thirties. It cost the various
governments in Canada tens of millions of dollars to buy feed to ship in to the farmers in the dried-out areas. If we could provide
75,000	small irrigation projects they would to a great extent ensure our farmery against crop failure; they would ensure our farmers adequate supplies of feed and make it unnecessary in the future for the government to spend millions of dollars on relief, to the embarrassment of all concerned.
I was going to refer in detail to the larger irrigation developments, but I shall make my remarks on that phase of the matter quite brief. It is estimated by Mr. George Spence that the cost of feasible irrigation projects in Saskatchewan would total some $86,000,000. It is estimated by the P.F.R.A. officials that the feasible projects in the prairies, including some possible developments in Alberta, would total about $111,000,000. Irrigation developments have many advantages, one of the most important being that they would provide a great deal of employment to people who are now unable to find work. We hear reports of tens of thousands of young Canadians who cannot find work. Going home last night on the street car, I overheard a conversation by a young returned soldier who had been discharged. He could not find a job and had no prospect of a job. He was single, and he went on to say that the married men were being given the preference. He had joined up in 1940 when he was quite young and had no experience in any particular line, and he found that experienced veterans were given the preference. I admit that that is just one case, but I think any one with foresight who looks into the near future will be dismayed at the prospects for full employment in Canada.
A few months ago the Minister of Reconstruction gave us a glowing report of the labour situation in Canada. He said that there were twice as many jobs as there were workers for the jobs. I wonder what the figures are to-day. I have been told that it is estimated that there are about 70,000 unemployed in Canada to-day. We should not consider irrigation projects solely from the point of view of whether they will pay or whether the government can hope to get back its investment. We are dealing with people and with the happiness of people. If we can provide irrigation facilities for thousands of farmers, we shall increase the happiness of thousands of people on those farms. If a veteran taking land in western Canada under the Veterans' Land Act knew that he could carry on irrigation even on a few acres, he would be more
Supply-Agriculture

willing to become a farmer and his chances of security on that farm would be much greater.
The government was given a mandate by the people of Canada, and that mandate to a large extent calls for jobs for all. I do not think the government should measure the money cost of jobs for all Canadians. In considering any comprehensive programme to provide full employment, the government must .get away from a niggardly figure of $2,000,000 for farm rehabilitation. Surveys that have been made to date by P.F.R.A. officials show that feasible programmes would cost something like $125,000,000. The cost of labour calculated into that estimate is at the rate of forty cents an hour, which I say is far too low. Wage rates should be increased for P.F.R.A. work. Possibly $150,000,000 is more like the outlay that should be made on the prairie farm rehabilitation programme, which, if spread over the next ten years, would mean an annual expenditure of $15,000,000.
I suggest that the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act be made to cover all Canada and that adequate surveys be made for proper land utilization throughout our nation. It may be that after these surveys have been made we shall need $50,000,000 a year for an adequate Canadian farm rehabilitation programme.

I should like to support my colleague, the hon. member for Cumberland, in his strong plea that something be done about the marshlands in Nova Scotia. The minister knows that there is not too great an area of land in Nova Scotia suitable for farming as farming is carried on to-day. Farming has changed in Nova Scotia the same as it has in many other places. The early settlers settled on the tops of hills so that they could see what was coming, but those farms have had to be abandoned. In many instances whole settlements and districts have had to be abandoned, and this has placed the rural population of Nova Scotia under great hardship. Our farms are now mostly concentrated along the river valleys and along the marshlands to which my colleague refers. I shall not speak about the river valleys at this time. They, too, have their problems at certain times of the year, and sooner or later something will have to be done to curb the flood waters on these rivers.
The marshlands in the counties of Cumberland, Colchester, Hants, Kings and Annapolis are the large producing areas in Nova Scotia. It is along these marshlands that the bulk of the farming is done. Years ago they were having a little problem keeping the dykes and sluices open and the drains dug, and keep-

ing the water off these areas. To-day some areas are having a great deal of difficulty and some of the land has been abandoned altogether. That is largely due to the fact that in the old days there were many men on the farms and in the communities roundabout who had been accustomed to putting in dykes and keeping the ditches open under the supervision of men who knew what they were doing, but these practical men are all gone now and there are few men left who understand the putting in of brush heaps and the building of dykes and sluices.
I suggest to the minister that what is required is an engineer who will study the situation and have working under him a group of men and the necessary machinery with which to do the work that is required. It is not an expensive project. No doubt it would take a little while to get such a crew organized and in operation. I do not suggest that the whole cost should be borne by the dominion government. I firmly believe that the property owners of the marshlands would be willing to bear their share, and I should like to see something of that kind set up. Then, when a sluice goes out or some drains have to be dug or brush heaps put in, the engineer could go and look over the situation and go ahead and do the work. I would suggest that the cost be borne in equal shares by. the federal Department of Agriculture, the provincial department of agriculture and by the marsh owners.
As I said before, the cost would not be so very big. In these days we are appropriating money for huge projects running almost into billions. Only the other day we were asked to approve a project whereby $750,000,000 would be devoted to the setting up of an international bank. It is hard for the ordinary person like myself to grasp such figures. But this project that I am advocating would not be expensive, and for the sake of the farmers of Nova Scotia along these fertile lands I would ask that the government grant a few thousand dollars to reclaim these marshlands. I do not think that is asking too much, and I urge the minister to take into consideration [DOT]the organization of a body of men under a competent engineer to take this work in hand.

The Minister of Agriculture is aware that there is a great deal of interest in the east central part of Alberta in a scheme known as the Red Deer river diversion scheme, which is a modification of the William Pearce project.
On October 1 last I moved for the production of papers containing a report on the progress of the surveys that had been made in connection with the scheme and I should like to

Supply-Agriculture
quote a paragraph from sessional paper No. 215 dealing with the possibilities of this project. It says:
This project will provide settlement, permanent homes and means of livelihood for 7,500 families in a section of western Canada from which over ninety per cent of the original settlers were forced by drought; it resettles an area now practically depopulated; the area will support between thirty and forty thousand people.
It will provide irrigation for approximately
500,000	acres of land suitable for irrigation. This land is not now in production and is largely publicly-owned. It will give constant flow to approximately 1,200 miles of dry creek channels traversing an area containing 12,000,000 acres of range lands and will materially increase the live stock carrying capacity of such lands.
It will rehabilitate twenty-four urban communities now practically depopulated from the years of drought.
The most important feature of this project will be stock watering rather than irrigation, because most of this land is used for grazing, and there is a. serious shortage of water in that area. During the past years of successive drought the rivers and lakes have dried up, and very few of the dug-outs are holding water to-day because there has been little or no run-off in the last few years. The dam built a few years ago held only enough water this year to let water down on the irrigated land just once. So that until water is diverted from the river into this area the situation will continue to be a serious one in years of short rainfall.
I asked when it was intended to develop this project, and the reply that was brought down was "not yet determined."
I should like to point out that the interest in this scheme is a lively one, and during the last election it reached fever height. The Liberal party certainly got the people so excited about this project that I had a hard job to persuade people in that area that work on this scheme had not already been started. When I announced that I hoped it would be started I was told that I was talking through my hat. Some people had. seen men working on the dam down the Red Deer river and thought that work on the scheme had actually started, but these men were only carrying on surveys. I am convinced that many people still believe that the scheme has been started, and they will be disappointed because it will not be started this year and in all probability will not be done next year and possibly the year after. But I express the hope to-night that work will be started in the very near future, because it is not in the category referred to by the hon. member for Calgary West. There is no question that, if put into operation, this scheme will be of immediate service to the farmers in the area. Unfortunately at the present time there seems to be a great deal of confusion between the federal government and the provincial government as to whose responsibility it is to make an investigation regarding the development of power. Paragraph (c) of the reply that was brought down to my question states:
The possibilities of power development are being investigated by the province of Alberta but no report on -the subject has been received -as yet by the dominion government.
That point was given a great deal of publicity in the newspapers throughout western Canada and I have received many inquiries. So I sent an airmail letter to the deputy minister of trade and industry in the government of Alberta to find out how far their investigation had gone. I should like to quote from that letter to show the minister the confusion that exists and to ask him whether he would not clarify the situation. The letter addressed to myself and dated Edmonton, December 4, 1945, reads:
Dear Mr. Queleh:
On receipt of your letter under date of November 22 asking for information on the proposed Red Deer diversion scheme I referred the same to Mr. B. Russell, director of water resources for the province.
You will perhaps remember that Mr. Russell before coming -to this government was, for a number of years, closely connected as -an engineer with the P.F.R.A. In fact for -a larger part of his experience he has been closely connected -and informed -regarding both irrigation and power possibilities in Alberta and Saskatchewan, -and I know of no one who can speak with closer authority from all angles in this matter, and particularly with regard to the best interest of the province of Alber-ta herein.
Mr. Russell has written -a complete memorandum summarizing the situation at present -as far as we know it in Alberta, this under date of November 28. Mr. Russell suggests that this memorandum will perhaps give you the -information -that you need, and I have pleasure in enclosing copy herewith.
I might say, and I am quite sure, that Alberta will be only too glad to make definite recommendations on the question of power developments or any other aspects of these proposals if -the necessary particulars were made available to -the proper officials of this government, with the intimation that the views of the province were desired.
Then he includes the recommendation and the submission by Mr. Russell, which I will now read:
I have your memorandum of the 26th to which is attached a letter dated November 22, from Victor Queleh, M.P.
The following is briefly a summary of the situation to date:
On March 5 -last, Mr. George Spence, director of P.F.R.A. wrote to -the Hon. D. B. MacMillan to which was -attached a sketch plan showing the -route now referred to by Mr, Queleh; the advantages -and other general data was also -attached.

Supply-Agriculture
Mr. Spence in his letter expressed the opinion that the P.F.R.A. had then gone about as far as it should go in its studies without having the consideration of the province and the usual application for investigation. Mr. MacMillan was requested to take this question under advisement.
In the material submitted, while power development was referred to, there was no indication as to- how such power could be developed, nor in fact any plans or information in sufficient detail from which any part of the proposal could be intelligently considered. We therefore wrote to Mr. Spence requesting certain additional plans and other material and at that time proposed other alternatives which we considered should be further investigated.
In the meantime, however, although we did not think that such a permit was necessary, we issued to the P.F.R.A. a preliminary permit required under the Water Resources Act to enter into and upon any lands for the purpose of making such investigations and surveys as may be necessary for the preparation of plans and estimates. I understand that these investigations are still in progress.
With regard to the power development particularly, this is a matter which has not yet been considered in sufficient detail either by the P.F.R.A. or the province to determine con-< clusively its feasibility, and we have no requests on file from the P.F.R.A. or any other body for permission to develop the water power -site.
The view of this department is that incidental to the development of irrigation from the Red Deer river there are very good possibilities for the development of water power and that no plan of irrigation which will destroy these power possibilities should be permitted. On the other hand, the P.F.R.A., while interested in the development of irrigation, is not much concerned with the power possibilities of the river. However, as a result of a conference I had with Mr. Gray and engineers of the P.F.R.A. last spring, a plan was discussed whereby the irrigation works could be so designed 'and located as to provide immediately the facilities for diverting water for irrigation without interfering with the power possibilities, but rather would create the conditions for power development later on when required. The P.F.R.A. undertook to make the necessary investigation and surveys to determine such possibilities but I have not yet received any report or plans from which to judge feasibility but I would infer from the paragraph quoted by Mr. Quelch that a combined irrigation and power development is now proposed. In this case the P.F.R.A. has never advised this office regarding this or requested the cooperation of the province with regard to power development or irrigation development.
The minister will note that in the concluding paragraph it states:
In this case the P.F.R.A. has never advised this office regarding this or requested the cooperation of the province with regard to power development or irrigation development.
Yet in the order tabled in the house it stated that "the possibilities of power development are being investigated by the province of Alberta but no report on the subject has been received as yet by the dominion government." There seems to be some con-

fusion there, and since there is so much interest in this question in Alberta I was wondering if the minister could say anything to clarify the situation. There seems to be some confusion as to whether the P.F.R.A. is conducting the investigation. Apparently the view of the province is that it is, while on the other hand the federal government appear to believe that the provincial government are conducting it. I think we should try to clarify that situation so that progress can be made. Can the minister give us some information?	*

I am ,just answering the questions that were asked with regard to it. My understanding is that the development of the Red Deer project will cost somewhere in the neighbourhood of $6,750,000, based on the same estimates which were referred to a few moments ago by the hon. member for Wood Mountain, and -which, he said, were at wage rates which he thought would be too low; so that if the wage rates there are increased in proportion to what he was suggesting, I suppose the cost would be considerably more than that.
The position which I understand exists there is this. Investigations have been made which indicate that there could be certain storages of water created, and that if you were to use all the water which is stored there for the purpose of developing power, it would reduce very little the amount of water which could be used for irrigation purposes; and vice versa; so that when one is talking about all the land which can be irrigated if you utilize all the water which can be stored in that dam, and then proceed to talk about all the power that can be developed if you use the water for the purpose of developing power, both things cannot be done to that extent.
It may be correct to say that nothing whatever has been, done to determine just how much power could be developed there, but I have had reports over a considerable period of time that certain power development could take place; but engineers are careful, as they ought to be, not to put their names to reports which would indicate that something can be done until they are definitely sure. As a matter of fact, the reports which we have are made by the same man who made the other reports. Our reports are made by Mr. Russell, who up to a few months ago was employed by us an-d who is now employed by the Alberta government. I assume that whatever information we have, they have, because the same man has done the work for both. I have not any reason for believing that the provincial government have gone any farther in considering a power development, but that they

Supply-Agriculture
simply took the figures which Mr. Russell has possession, of, as we have possession of them, and which indicate that a certain amount of power could be developed there, and to that extent they are probably giving consideration to it. We are giving consideration to it to the same extent.
One or two projects are taking precedence over that project at the present time. One is the St. Mary's project in the southern part of Alberta, for which we hope to get some money voted in supplementaries in the present year. We shall not be able to spend all we get in the supplementaries because of the nearness of the end of the financial year, but we hope to get sufficient to make a start, and have a revote, if we are not able to spend it all, in the succeeding year to go on with that development.
Would the Minister of Agriculture give us an idea of about how much he expects to have appropriated this year?

I would rather wait until the supplementary comes down. I know how much we have recommended, and I think the amount we have recommended will be in it. But we shall not be able to spend as much as we got this year.
When does the minister expect that to come in?
Well, the supplementaries will be in in a few days, if we expect to get through by the end of next week.

The people in that part of the country realize that the St. Mary's power project will have priority, on account of the international situation; but can the minister say that there is every reason to believe that when that project is completed the federal government will be proceeding with the Red Deer development scheme? That would be some encouragement.

I would say that that is one which is on the list to be given consideration at as early a day as possible. I do not know just when that day will be; it depends on so many things, the amount of labour available and the question of making final engineering explorations in connection with it. It is just possible that when we get to the stage of making our report, those who have to take the responsibility for supplying the money will say, "We want another firm of engineers", or something like that, before we proceed with the work. If they do so, it will 47696-201	.
take longer; therefore I am not in a position to say when we shall start, but we shall start as soon as possible.

I was not suggesting for one minute that there was any friction between the federal and provincial governments. Is the federal government depending upon the provincial government for making any further investigation in relation to power development, because it will be noted that in the letter from Mr. Russell, he states:
However, as a result of a conference I had with Mr. Gray and engineers of the P.F.R.A. last spring, a plan was discussed whereby the irrigation works could be so designed and located as to provide immediately the facilities for diverting water for irrigation without interfering, with the power possibilities.
Apparently they have found a scheme whereby both irrigation and power development can be carried out. Am I to understand that as far as the power development is concerned the minister is expecting the provinces to carry out that investigation and P.F.R.A. will only proceed with the work of irrigation?

I would not say definitely that is the case. So far as I am personally concerned I think the more authority that those who are providing the money have in connection with matters of this kind to create the work that they do themselves, the more likely the thing is to be done. I find in negotiating with two or three different authorities that it takes just about three times as long to get started.
The minister will be investigating the whole thing?

I think what should be done in this instance is that we should discuss the matter with the provincial governments. We should find out definitely whether they would utilize in some way or another the water supplies that we provide them. Then we should proceed up to a certain point in making the storage of water possible, put the storages there. After that, we can deal with whatever authority is going to use the water; it may be a provincial authority; it may be simply the local irrigation organization set up for that purpose. But I would think that if we simply tied it up to a definite agreement between this government and the provincial governments, it would slow the matter up. All we want is to get along with it as quickly as possible. I would hesitate to say that we are 'going to make an investigation in regard to power development

Supply-Agriculture

for the provinces. I would hesitate to say we shall not do it if the provinces want us to undertake it.

May I ask one question arising out of what has been said about power development on the Red Deer river? I know the Red Deer river very well. There is a gradual slope through the prairies. Has any investigation been made to show that you can get power from water storage anywhere on that river cheaper than you can get it right now in the town of Drumheller which is using this waste or slack coal? It is all right to talk about power from water storage. I am very much of an amateur in this business, but I have very grave doubt of any power scheme on the Red Deer which could produce power as cheaply as it is now produced at the power pla*nt which is using this waste or slack coal at the present time. Has any investigation been made?

That is a question which has to have great consideration. I do not think there is any doubt in anyone's mind that you can develop power on the Red Deer river by spending a certain amount of money. Reports have been made on that from time to time. But th'en the question arises, as has just been indicated, as to whether the money ought to be spent there for the development, of power. I think it is admitted by all that you could spend money there to good advantage to develop irrigation.
That is, my thought.

I think that is pretty well proven. If we have to decide the question now as to whether the government ought to use that, water for irrigation or power we would say, use it for irrigation; and I would be quite certain that if it did develop that as a result of the investigation which had been made you could develop that power cheaper in the town of Drumheller with the use of coal, that would be the deciding factor. I would think that if you develop it cheaper than by the use of water we would use the water for irrigation, and use the other for power. Those are the things that I do not think are fully determined, and we would not proceed to provide for the development of power until they were fully determined.

In other
words, do you think it possible that you could do both from the water? Irrigation means that you mu-t take water from a high place and spread it over some place lower. Power from

water means that you have the weight of the water coming from a high place to a low place. Perhaps that is an amateur's way of putting it, but it seems to me it is a simple fact. Does the department think you can build dams where you can do both things? I would have a bit of a doubt about it.
I point out that in earlier surveys it was shown that there could be power developments from the water developments on the Saskatchewan and Clearwater rivers.
That was called a stock-watering scheme.
Yes, I think it provided for irrigation of one and a half million acres.
Yes, that was the William Pearce scheme.
Yes, but it provided for a power development.

It seems to me that almost everyone in the house to-night is anxious to inform the minister on various situations pertaining to water conservation and irrigation throughout the country. Some of the speeches have given instructions. It is not my purpose to add to that number. I wish to ask the minister one or two questions pertaining to a project which is partly in my constituency, and which is of direct concern to Regina. Is he prepared to-night to say whether or not there have been any recent developments in connection with the water conservation project which is located south of the Wascana creek involving an area which we know as the Tyvan area? As the hon. member
knows, the Wascana scheme has been under consideration for a long time, almost as long as the project referred to by the hon. member for Calgary West, who must have been standing very close to where I was standing many years ago, because I was standing there when they turned on the' tap and let the water into the reservoir at Regina. At that time his father was mayor of the city. This other thing has been talked about for almost as long as they have been talking about the water up in the Wascana in order to replenish the water in the artificial lake at Regina. That was the first use they pro-

posed to make of it. We have got right up to the point of the building of the dam there so often and then have decided not to build it that I should not like to make any promises at this time. I support the request made of the minister by the hon. member for Cumberland and the hon. member for Col-chester-Hants for assistance to reclaim the marshlands and to rebuild the dykes in 'New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. In passing, may I say that the first of those dykes was built a great many years ago by settlers from old France who came into what was then Acadia. Longfellow in his peom "Evangeline" refers to these dykes and marshlands.
In the Acadian land, on the shores of the Basin of Minas,
Distant, secluded, still, the little village of Grand-Pre
Lay in the fruitful valley. Vast meadows stretched to the eastward,
Giving the village its name, and pasture to flocks without number.
Dykes, that the hands of the farmers had raised with labor incessant,
Shut out the turbulent tides; hut at stated
seasons the flood-gates
Opened, and welcomed the sea to wander at will o'er the meadows.
These are the dykes and meadows that have been referred to this evening.
During the course of his remarks one hon. gentleman mentioned the aboideaux, which are gates in the dykes that permit the water to run off the marshlands but stop the sea from running in. I refer to it in passing because the word "aboideau" is perhaps the one word that has been contributed to the English language by the province of New Brunswick. If you will look at the word in sbme of our dictionaries you will find that it has become an English word and that it originated in New Brunswick.
47696-201i
Some of those lands and dykes are situated in the constituency which I have the honour to represent. It is a sad sight to drive along a road in the county of Albert and look down over these marshlands. You should see green, fertile fields, but actually you see nothing but a brown, muddy waste. I drove through what is known as the parish of Harvey not very long ago. I stopped my car and looked out over the marshes. The tide was high and I counted twenty-four bams completely surrounded by water, which of course meant that those meadow lands were of no further use. The hon. member for Colchester-Hants has referred briefly to the reasons for these marshlands and dykes going down. I do not propose to pursue that line of thought, but I should like to state briefly my own views as to what should be done.
It seems to me that if these lands are to be brought under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, or any similar act, it will be necessary to show that the money spent by the dominion government will be a reasonably sound expenditure economically,- taking a long view of it. My own feeling in the matter is that it will do no good1 for the dominion government to spend a great deal of money in reclaiming dykes unless some plan is worked out for the proper use of the land after it has been reclaimed. Unless enterprise and cooperation are shown by the owners of the land; unless the provincial governments are prepared to assist the scheme and help develop a plan that will make these lands of economic value, it does not seem to me there is much use in the dominion government going in and spending a great deal of money, for it will be only thrown away.
If this plan is to be successful there must be cooperation between the owners of the land, the provinces concerned and the dominion government. I understand that last year in New Brunswick about 5,000 feet of dyke were. constructed under a plan whereby the owners paid one-third of the cost, the provincial government paid one-third and the dominion government paid one-third, and that this year about a similar length of dyke has been constructed under the same plan. If I am wrong in that, perhaps the minister will inform me.
That is right.

If the dyke owner himself is willing to put his money into the scheme it seems to me it shows he is really interested and is prepared to do his bit to make the lands of value again. But I think we have to go farther than the owners of the lands themselves. The provincial and dominion govern-
Supply-Agriculture

meats have to work out a plan if the money expended is to produce results and not be wasted.
Something else must be done as well. The marsh acts, as they are sometimes called, or the marsh laws in the provinces have to be revised, codified, brought up to date and made workable, so that once the dykes are rebuilt they will be maintained. The regulations must be such that one dyke owner cannot say, "Well, I am not going to pay," and have the thing drag on so that finally the dyke commences to deteriorate. Unless a better commission is set up or somebody has power to deal with the; dyke laws and see that they are properly enforced, we are not going to get anywhere.
These are just one or two suggestions I am offering to the minister. I think it is almost a crime to see these productive lands being destroyed and' going to waste, and that process seems to be continuing. But I believe the only way to bring them back is through cooperation between the owners, the provincial governments and1 the dominion government. It will be no good for the dominion government just to put money in there by itself; the provincial government and the land owners themselves must be ready to cooperate.
I was going to ask the minister one other question about this item, if I may.( The total amount is $2,000,000. Of this I see that wages account for $671,000, including temporary assistance and so on; buildings and lands, $621,000, travelling expenses, $186,000, and so on. How much of the money voted for prairie farm rehabilitation was actually spent in doing the work of putting in these small or large water developments? About how much of the total was actually spent for that purpose?

The amount voted
annually during the war years has been $2,000,000, and approximately thei whole amount has been spent each year. What are called wages and, to a certain extent, salaries are really part of the work.
That includes labour?

Yes, it includes the labour and the engineering. The engineering has to be Carried out first, together with some exploration. All that is really part of the cost of the projects which are carried out. I could give the exact figures, but I do not think that is necessary.
I do not want the details. What is covered under "buildings and lands"?

We have to put up buildings in connection with many of the projects, and we have to buy lands where we are going to flood them. When we dig ditches

in order to carry water through the land of other people, we have to buy the right of way. All that involves the purchasing of land and sometimes even of buildings. In some cases we have put up the buildings. If one were to describe the different projects this would be fully understood.
The discussion this evening has led me to review in my own mind the meaning of the term "can be constructed economically." If it means what most people have in mind when they use it, I would suggest that if the government were to take that as its reason for starting any of these projects we would never start. For example, we had a statement made a few moments ago by the hon. member for Calgary West, and everything he said was absolutely correct. The Canadian Pacific built an irrigation system at Brooks and tried to run it as a purely business proposition. They lost money all the time. They tried; when they sold land to a farmer, to charge a price which eventually would pay for the project, so that if the farmer made his payments year by year, and paid his water rates, eventually they would get their money back. They found that could not be done, and that has been found in every scheme of irrigation ever tried. It is the case in the United States and in all our plans. We have found this-and it is the basis on which we work-that you cannot charge a farmer more than $10 an acre for land which you will irrigate and then charge for water and expect him to pay for it. That is the basis on which the Brooks scheme is now operated by the farmers to whom it was turned over by the Canadian Pacific.

At $1 an
acre; they raised the ante.

Yes. They were given
$400,000 to take it.

They are
charging $1 an acre instead of fifty cents.

The people there will
sell land for $10 an acre. We went south of that project. We found 50,000 acres of land south of the Brooks project, owned by that organization. We took over those 50,000 acres. We could put water on 25,000 acres because there was only half of the land there of such a level that water could be put on it.
Irrigable.

Yes; we put water on
25,000 acres and we said to the farmers: "If you were ordinary farmers you would have to pay $10 an acre, but we will take steps which

Supply-At/riculture
will warrant the Brooks set-up in selling the land to you at $8 an acre." In other words, we put up 82 an acre.

Does the minister
mean $8 for the land with water right?

They had to pay for
the water from the Brooks project. They pay a water rate, but they get the land at $8 an acre. We went into the drought area and did just what the hon. member for Wood Mountain said we ought to do. We persuaded the farmers to move away from that place, actually driving them from where they were to the rolling hills area. We showed them the set-up there, and we said to them, "If you want to go there, if you want to get out of this drought area, we will take down your buildings and move them for you. We will stand the expense of moving your equipment and buildings from where you are to the place where you want to go, and we will pay you $8 an acre,when you get there." That place has been filled by people who have moved from the places they occupied previously. When I was last there I saw buildings of various colours because the boards had been taken out of the old buildings and were utilized in putting up new structures, and they had not been painted.

They are
doing very well.

Yes; they are doing
very well. There are two or three kickers, but you get them anywhere. There are one or two who have not made good, but the great majority of the people there have succeeded and they would not go back to any other district.. But you cannot put that on an economic basis and say that if you spend so much money on the land you will have to get it back within so many years.
You get it back in taxes,

The point can be better illustrated by taking the marshlands. If we did what they wanted us to do on the marshlands it would cost from $125 to 8150 an acre, and if you went into that district and asked anyone if he was prepared to buy the land there at that price he would say no. If you wait until you get into the position where the position is considered economic you will not do anything at all, but we have done some experimenting there. It was started under Mr. Bennett's government and I was in that district the first year I took over the department.. I found that they had reached the point of taking over the land. I was confronted with making the decision whether we
would go ahead, and we took so many acres of land alongside the experimental farm of X'appan and developed the same programme that anyone would have to develop on the rest of it to improve the land. My information is that the land was producing three-quarters per ton per acre of alfalfa and other hays when it was left alone. Under our experimentation we are producing four tons to the acre. In other words, the economic decision from my point of veiw, is that you can increase production of that land from three-quarters of a ton per acre up to four tons by treating	it in	certain	ways,	and	thelast time	I was	there	I was	surprised.	To
stand and look at the land across the road would make one weep to think that people could put up with a condition such as that without doing something about it when they compared it with what was taking place right opposite them.
The same thing is true of Valmarie. There were some people in that district who would not allow	us to	touch	their	land.	In	1937that land	was as	bare	as this	floor.	On	one
side of the road there was land growing forty bushels to the acre, and on the other side it was all bare notwithstanding the fact that the people there ha'd a demonstration of what could actually be done. I was there last summer and some of that land is still black and the people who own it are sitting there.
The point is that we have to get men who are inspired with the possibilities of what can be done on any of these schemes if you are to accomplish something.
Let me now take a third one, the muck-lands. This is something that affects the central provinces, and I may say that as far as I am concerned it may be called a ghost story. I have recollections of that land when I lived in Ontario as a boy. When I lived here as a boy I lived on a road where there was a swamp, and the thing I remember most about it was the stories I heard men telling about the will-o'-the-wisp they saw in the sw'amp and about pulling horses and cattle out of the muck in that swamp. Men delighted in telling exaggerated stories, and the result was that when I went by that swamp, especially at night, I ran past it.
And there was no General Chisholm.

What has happened to that land, however, the transformation that has taken place in it, is no ghost story, and perhaps I might mention a name which some people may not like. But anyone who wants to see what can be done with muckland should visit the farm of Mitch Hepburn.

In Kent county.
Supply-Agriculture
I was there on Friday.

My hon. friend will
know that there is a bit of muekland there out of which they used to pull horses. They used to spend Sunday afternoon pulling horses and cattle out of that' muck. That land was absolutely useless as muekland because it entailed work and yielded nothing. Well, the last time I was there I saw sixty men engaged in growing onions and other things on that land. That is the difference to-day. Between forty and fifty acres of land . had lain there black, saturated with water, humid soil that would grow vegetables as nothing else would, and yet it had been left there for generations without having anything done about it. He has drained the water out of that land and provided a water supply for the protection of the buildings which is just as good fire protection as afforded in any city in Canada. Moreover, he has an artificial lake where he can have a summer resort at home. And the water is running out of the mucklands past his own buildings down to the lake, creating a beauty spot on the farm.
That kind of thing can be duplicated all over Ontario and Quebec. Instead of having three or four men in an area tfying to raise a few steers and hogs such as we have been talking about, you could have sixty men working a garden and producing other necessaries of life, and they could make as much money and live as good a life as those three or four who were doing limited work on the same area.
These are the considerations we ought to have in our minds when we are discussing the subject and not merely what the land will be worth per acre. These works that will be put in to protect the marshlands in the maritimes will do something to improve land that would stay there 100 years without having anything done to them. It is not a question what that land will be worth next year if it is sold; it is a question of what it will be worth, not only to that community but to the Dominion of Canada for the next 100 years. In other words, one has to get the same vision that Theodore Roosevelt had in the United States at the time he was president. He had lived as a cowboy out in the western part of the United States and he knew what that-country could be developed into. When he became President of the United States he said what I think needs saying here. He said, "There have been millions upon millions of dollars spent in building harbours to make it possible for ships
['Mr. MacNieol.]
to come in to get the commodities of this country; there have been millions of dollars spent to build stations for railways and all that kind of thing; we ought to spend millions of dollars in order to make it possible to produce more commodities to pass through these ports and over these railways." If we get that kind of vision, then I think all the things we have been talking about to-night ought to be done by somebody. I agree with the hon. member who says that lye ought to have some discussion with regard to it. We are having that discussion now with the provinces in the dominion-provincial conference that is being held from time to time.
I hope we shall get around to considering the whole question. I assure the hon. member for Davenport that there is no one in the House of Commons who will ask for more money than I have asked for already. Ten years ago when we were discussing the same matter it took me three days to get the bill through the house which provided for the spending of a very small sum of money upon P.F.R.A. projects. Hon. members who were here then will recall that when I tried to increase the sum from $4,750,000 and provide that it be unlimited, I had to discuss the question for more than a day. I was asked, "What are you going to do with all that money? How much money is it going to take?"
"Where are you going to get the money?"

I do not know that they said, "Where are you going to get the money?" But they said, "What are you going to do with it when you do get it?" "How much are you going to want?" I said I wanted at least $20,000,000. "When are you going to want it?" I said I wanted it just as fast as they would give it to me and I would take it at whatever rate they would give it to me. I am now standing here ten years later. We have spent $20,000,000 and I have not heard one word of criticism to-night about that expenditure. You have simply said that we have not spent enough and you want to spend more. There never was $20,000,000 spent in this country that gave more satisfaction to the people where it was spent than that $20,000,000. If we spend $100,000,000 over a period of time, as has been suggested by the hon. member for Davenport, I am sure the same thing will be said at the end of that time.
I appreciate the fact that every one who has risen to-night to speak on this item has urged that more money be spent than we are proposing to spend and that we ought to

Supply*-Agriculture
spend it in all parts of Canada rather than in one section only. I hope in due course we shall be able to do that.

I should like to correct one statement the minister made. He said that the cost would be from $125 to $150 per acre but that would apply only to certain small areas and not to- the entire 100,000 or 150,000 acres of marshland.

The acreage is 69,000
acres and the proposed cost is $4,000,000. The hon. member can figure it out for himself.

I am not going to take up very much time because other hon. members have dealt most ably with this matter. After hearing the remarks of the minister, I about came to the conclusion that I would not have to say anything at all. I was glad to hear what he had to say. I know of nothing that would be of greater national importance and of more lasting value than this water storage we have been talking about tonight. I would be prepared to multiply many times the amount to be spent. I think the spending of a billion dollars would be the best kind of investment for Canada.
I come from a part of the country that has had some benefit from this water storage, and I think it is the finest thing that was ever introduced into that part of the country. I should like to ask the minister if he has in mind as a future programme the continuation of the irrigation projects at Eastend, Valmarie and Maple Creek. I think every drop of water that is stored in western Canada is of real value. It raises the water level in the wells of the farmers. At the present time wells are beginning to run dry, and I should like to know if the minister intends developing these projects.

Of course there are
some projects where you reach the point where you cannot do much more. In irrigation you can only use the water you have. As my hon. friend well knows, under the irrigation plan at Maple Creek we were only able to flood the land there once this year. If we had been able to flood it twice we would have been able to grow two crops of alfalfa instead of one. All the water stored at Maple Creek has been used this year, and it would be foolish for us to enlarge the area unless we could get more water.
In the Eastend scheme we have dammed the waters of Cypress lake and we have raised the level some eight or ten feet. Dams were constructed at both ends of the lake. When I was at Valmarie or Eastend this year I was a little worried about the water supply. We
were irrigating practically the whole valley at Eastend and Valmarie, and there are some six thousand acres under irrigation at the bottom of the dam. We used most of the water that was available this year, and I think nearly all the land that we can irrigate in the Valmarie district is under irrigation. Most of the land that we can irrigate at Eastend is under irrigation as well. I do not know that it is a case of further development there. There are other places where further development might be carried on.
We are certainly going to continue what we are doing there. We are going to grow alfalfa at all these places. These projects were started to make it certain that people could live in that country no matter how dry a year there was. When I went there this year I found the country dried up, and I found those who were in charge of the plots on which water had been put trucking hay out of the area. They were going up the road as I was coming down to look at it. They were taking the hay into Swift Current and other places where it was to be shipped away to make powdered protein feeds. That was not the purpose of making that irrigated area., The purpose of putting irrigation there was to make it possible for people to raise live stock and live there themselves.
I was delighted the other day when a young man wrote to me who was just back from overseas. Most hon. members would know the family if I mentioned his name. This man said that he had been in training at Medicine Hat during the war and had definitely made up his mind to come back to start farming in the Medicine Hat district. He said that he understood there would be an irrigation scheme started there, and it is under discussion. He said. "I was disappointed when I came back to find that it had not been started." He wrote me to say that his vision was a home on an irrigated piece of land in that country, with a large pasture near it into which he could turn his cattle. He wanted to raise cattle in that way, and he is one of the most capable producers of cattle we have in western Canada. I wrote back to him and said: "You go down to Regina and get Spence to drive you out to Valmarie and Eastend. Ever since this project has been put in I have been wanting young fellows with just the vision this young man has, and I told him that if he would start farming out there it would not be long before twenty or thirty or forty other young fellows would be out there doing the same.

Has the land been
taken up?
Supply-Agriculture

Yes; it has been used
for growing alfalfa, which was put up in bales and shipped out to plants and made into something else. I hoped that this young man would go there and take a quarter-section of land to grow feed for his live stock. We have 110,000 acres of pasture right alongside that is all fenced in and with water on it for live stock. I want him to go out there, take a piece of land, go on it and live there, turn his cattle into the pasture, and pay the small fee for running his cattle there. That is the dream I have had in mind for that part of the country, and I hope that many of these young fellows who come back will take advantage of it.

In the southern part of
Saskatchewan, as the minister knows, there is considerable submarginal land. What acreage of this submarginal land has been taken out of production and placed in community pasture, and is that programme to be extended there?

Approximately 1,350,000 acres have been taken out, but not all taken out of cultivation. Part of it was being used for pasturing in the form of ranches. We have taken that land over, fenced it in and made absolutely certain-in fact we have title to the land-that it will not be broken up again and will not be pastured to the extent it had been pastured, where it looked almost 'ike summer fallow.

I should like to express to the minister the gratitude of my constituency for the construction of the Leavitt irrigation district west of Cardston. I am also informed that the contract has been let for the construction of the Aetna irrigation district? Is that correct?
Yes.

I wish to express our gratitude for that project and to tell the minister in the presence of the committee that these two projects will be successful. The Leavitt project has been successful, and generations after generations will be blessing the minister for making the necessary expenditure under P.F.R.A. for bringing water into an otherwise fertile area which occasionally suffered because of a shortage of rainfall. The same will be true of the Aetna project.

Is consideration being
given to the application of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act on an individual basis? If the answer is yes, I need say no more.
* [Mr, Gardiner.!

Consideration was given to it at the time the scheme was first set up, but it was found impossible to apply it in that way. Our constitution does not permit of it. To apply it on an individual basis, it would have to be on an insurance plan, and that is impossible even if it were desirable The position we take is that even if it were possible we doubt the advisability of it. The people of Canada are putting three dollars into that project for every one dollar that is paid in by the people concerned, and in order to persuade them to do that we have had to suggest to them that we are not encouraging people to stay on submarginal land. We are not condemning the man living right in the middle of a district who, because of his methods, produces when other people do not. But instead of putting it on an individual basis we put it on the basis of a block of land and say that everybody in that block will be treated alike under the weather conditions that prevail throughout the year. I could not have got the bill through council or through the house in any other way.

I am not quite satisfied with the minister's explanation. I am not blaming him for the conclusions he has ardved at. I know some of the difficulties he has in administering the plan. At the same time his conclusions are not correct when he says that some people by their methods of farming can produce crops when others are not doing so. I know the part of the country from which I come pretty well, and the lay of the land sometimes makes all the difference between having a shower. If hon gentlemen will look at this map which I have here, it shows one township on the south side of the Saskatchewan river, with highway No. -1 running through it. The white spaces on the map indicate the crop land of that year, 1941; th black spaces, the summer fallow; the green spaces, the pasture land; and the red spaces are the low crop farms of that year. Where the crop failure was is marked red on the map. Some of the land is pasture land. In the township there are thirty-eight farmers. Of those thirty-eight farmers, four had 13-4 bushels to the acre; twelve had 7T1 bushels to the acre, and twenty-two had 3-18 bushels to the acre.
That is all wheat? Does it include wheat or everything?
There were practically no coarse grains that year.

That is the whole point. The payments are not paid on the basis of

wheat at all. I do not know why people will not study the act and really know what it means.
Pardon me; that was an error. This gives the total crop production in 1941.
The estimate is made on the wheat production. That is only to show how dry it was.
Oh, no.
It is. I know. I have been administering the act ever since it was set up. I drew it up in the first place.

Very well; we will take your word for it. The total crop average was 5-5 bushels to the acre, and twenty-two farmers having less than that had to suffer because the average was over five bushels to the acre. It is not a bad piece of land. There are a lot of good farmers there, and when they get rain they can produce a crop. In the years when they do not get rain they have to have something to carry them over. That is the whole purpose of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, to carry people in these semi-arid areas when they do not produce a crop.
Is that between Saskatchewan Landing and Swift Current?
Yes.
That could be irrigated from the dam on the Saskatchewan river.

I shall not go into that, because it is a big project and it would take time to discuss it. I am not asking the minister to enter into a debate with me about this to-night, but to consider taking it to the dominion-provincial conference or to initiate b3T any other method discussions with the provinces to introduce a crop insurance measure. If that requires provincial legislation, make arrangements for it to be done. If it requires that the farmers pay the cost, make that necessary to be done also. \Ve do not ask the people of eastern Canada to do this job on a crop insurance plan.
It cannot be done in any other way.
Very well; I believe it can, if you can maintain the present price level. *
Some people tried for forty years to do it in that way and it could not be done. Statistics were produced every time it was brought up, and it was turned down. It operates in this way-
It operates as a relief plan, to take people off relief.
No, it does not.

That is what it is, nothing more or less than a relief plan. It takes them off the municipal relief roll and puts them on relief in this way. So far as any investigation is concerned, that is a matter of opinion also. You can have other data which will cause you to come to a different conclusion. The point I wish to get at is this: If you can stabilize agricultural prices somewhere near what is being asked for and where some of them are at the present time, it is possible for the farmers to pay enough that you will not need to charge the rest of the dominion the other $3 to provide something for a plan of this kind, nor would you find it necessary to charge them to put in an actual crop insurance plan, based oh something better than relief figures.
What percentage would you suggest they should be charged?
It depends entirely on what you, your government, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and so on, decide are the proper price levels over a period of years.
How much do you think could be collected?
If you were to assure the farmers of the west that the price of their wheat would never fall below $1.25 a bushel, not many would raise much complaint if the charge was 10 cents.
Ten cents for what?
I do not think you will need that much. It has not been tried.
You would have to have about 20 cents to do what we are doing now.
I do not think so.

With respect to this item I should like to know when it is expected that finality will be reached in the matter of wheat acreage reduction payments. through to date. Would the minister give us an estimate, at least, of when these payments will be made and when this matter will be finally cleared up?
